meta.blurb: On Rachel Verinder's birthday, a yellow diamond is locked in a cabinet. By morning it is gone, and the only clue is a smear on a wet door. Three strangers watch the house, and a famous detective arrives to find the thief.
meta.bible: Moonstone: a large yellow diamond, once set in the forehead of a Hindu statue of the moon god; its light is said to rise and fall with the moon. Seringapatam: the Indian fortress where the diamond was taken in 1799. Colonel John Herncastle: the soldier who took it; Lady Verinder's hated brother; he leaves it in his will to Rachel. Lady Julia Verinder: Rachel's kind, sensible mother. Rachel Verinder: her proud, secretive daughter, eighteen on 21 June 1848. Gabriel Betteredge: the old house steward, a fan of Robinson Crusoe; he tells the first part. Penelope: Betteredge's daughter and Rachel's maid. Franklin Blake: Rachel's clever, well-travelled cousin, who brings the diamond to the house. Godfrey Ablewhite: another cousin, a charming public speaker for good causes, secretly deep in debt. Rosanna Spearman: a housemaid, once a thief, who loves Franklin. Lucy Yolland: a fisherman's daughter and Rosanna's friend. Superintendent Seegrave: the clumsy local policeman. Sergeant Cuff: the famous London detective who loves roses. Mr Murthwaite: a traveller who knows India well. Dr Candy: the local doctor, fond of jokes. Miss Clack: Rachel's pious cousin, who tells the London part. Mr Bruff: the family lawyer. Mr Luker: a London moneylender. Ezra Jennings: Dr Candy's gentle, sick assistant with two-coloured hair. Three Indians: Brahmin priests who follow the diamond, first seen as street jugglers. Yorkshire: the county of Lady Verinder's house. Frizinghall: the nearby town. The Shivering Sand: a deadly quicksand by the sea. London. India. Kattiawar: the part of India where the diamond finally returns. Voice and tone: a classic mystery told by several witnesses in turn; warm, wry, full of surprises; deaths are stated plainly, with no gore. The secret: Franklin, given laudanum without knowing it, took the diamond in his sleep; Godfrey then took it from him. Tipu Sultan: the ruler whose fortress fell in 1799. Brahmin: a Hindu priest. Montagu Square: the London street where Lady Verinder takes a house. Dorking: the town where Sergeant Cuff grows roses. Gooseberry: a boy who helps Sergeant Cuff. Mrs Ablewhite: Godfrey's mother, who lives in Frizinghall. Mr Begbie: the Verinder gardener. Mr Ablewhite: Godfrey's father. Northwood: a village near London. Lambeth: the part of London where Mr Luker lives. Lombard Street: the London street of the bank. Somnauth: the holy city where the diamond comes to rest. Tolliver's: the London inn where Godfrey hides. Robinson Crusoe: Betteredge's favourite book. Thursday: the day after the birthday. Samuel: a footman at Lady Verinder's house, who helps Betteredge on his rounds. The experiment: a year after the birthday Franklin takes a false yellow stone from the cabinet in his sleep, watched by Ezra Jennings, Mr Bruff and Rachel. Godfrey repays Mr Luker and takes the diamond from the Lombard Street bank; the three Indians take it from him at Tolliver's inn.
chapters: The Last Journey of the Stone

beats.scene: A great yellow diamond glows in the forehead of a moon god's statue
beats.summary: In India, a sacred yellow diamond shines in the forehead of a statue of the moon god.

beats.scene: Three priests in white robes keep watch by lamplight beside the statue
beats.summary: Three Brahmin priests are sworn to guard the diamond, and their sons will guard it after them.

beats.scene: A priest tells a warning to a pilgrim beneath a temple lamp
beats.summary: A legend warns that whoever takes the diamond by force will bring misfortune on himself and his family.

beats.scene: Armed men carry a loaded treasure chest through a stone gateway
beats.summary: Over the years the diamond passes through wars and ends up in the fortress of Seringapatam.

beats.scene: English soldiers storm the broken wall of a fortress under a smoky sky
beats.summary: In May 1799 the English army attacks Seringapatam and breaks into the fortress.

beats.scene: A young officer slips alone through a dark palace corridor
beats.summary: A young English officer, John Herncastle, goes looking for the diamond in the confusion.

beats.scene: A soldier holds the glowing diamond in a dim room
beats.summary: Herncastle takes the diamond, and men die that night.

beats.scene: A grim soldier stands alone while relatives turn away in a London street
beats.summary: Herncastle returns to England, and his family and friends keep away from him.

beats.scene: A lonely man sits behind locked doors in a dim London house
beats.summary: The Colonel lives alone in London for years, afraid of the Indians.

beats.scene: A lawyer reads a will aloud to Lady Verinder and her young daughter
beats.summary: The Colonel dies in 1848 and his will leaves the diamond to Rachel on her eighteenth birthday; Franklin Blake is to bring it.

beats.scene: An old steward in a black coat writes at a desk with a pipe
beats.summary: Gabriel Betteredge, now an old man, sits down to write what he remembers of the lost diamond.

beats.scene: A worn copy of Robinson Crusoe lies open on a kitchen table
beats.summary: Betteredge trusts his old copy of Robinson Crusoe for advice about every trouble in life.

beats.scene: A large grey house stands among green fields beside the sea
beats.summary: Lady Verinder's great house stands in Yorkshire, near the sea, and Betteredge has served it for fifty years.

beats.scene: A kind widow in a plain dress speaks warmly to a servant
beats.summary: Lady Julia Verinder is a kind, sensible widow who runs her household calmly.

beats.scene: A proud young girl in a white dress stands in the garden
beats.summary: Rachel Verinder, the only daughter, is proud, warm-hearted and not yet eighteen.

beats.scene: A cheerful maid in an apron chatters while sewing in a bright room
beats.summary: Penelope, Betteredge's daughter, is Rachel's maid and brings her father all the news of the house.

beats.scene: A pale young woman in a plain servant's dress stands at a window
beats.summary: The housemaid Rosanna Spearman was once a thief, and Lady Verinder gave her a second chance.

beats.scene: A lonely girl in a plain dress sews alone in a quiet room
beats.summary: Rosanna is shy and plain, with one shoulder higher than the other, and she keeps away from the other maids.

beats.scene: A wide beach with two rocky points and a smooth, shining sand between them
beats.summary: The Shivering Sand is a deadly quicksand between two rocky points on the shore.

beats.scene: Rosanna sits alone on a rock above the sand as waves roll in
beats.summary: Rosanna often sits alone on a rock above the Shivering Sand, and Betteredge worries about her.

beats.scene: Betteredge reads a letter at a kitchen table while Lady Verinder listens
beats.summary: A letter tells the household that Franklin Blake is coming to stay.

beats.scene: A smiling young man in a travelling coat looks at maps and books
beats.summary: Franklin grew up abroad and has a French side, a German side and an Italian side.

beats.scene: Lady Verinder frowns over the Colonel's letter beside her daughter
beats.summary: Lady Verinder learns that Franklin will bring the Colonel's diamond, and Rachel is excited.

beats.scene: Penelope runs across the yard, pointing at three men in white at the gate
beats.summary: One afternoon, three Indian jugglers arrive at the door.

beats.scene: An Indian juggler tosses glittering balls in the sunny yard
beats.summary: The jugglers perform tricks with brass balls, and the household gathers to watch.

beats.scene: An Indian pours ink into a boy's palm and speaks softly
beats.summary: The leader pours ink into the boy's hand and asks about an English gentleman coming from foreign parts.

beats.scene: Betteredge points to the gate while the three men bow politely
beats.summary: Betteredge sends the men away, but he cannot forget their calm, polite faces.

beats.scene: A young man in a travelling coat steps from a carriage
beats.summary: Franklin Blake arrives at the house, cheerful and tired from the journey.

beats.scene: Franklin tells Betteredge about the diamond while Lady Verinder listens
beats.summary: Franklin says he left the diamond in a bank in Frizinghall and that Indians followed him.

beats.scene: Franklin and Betteredge talk gravely by lamplight in the study
beats.summary: Betteredge tells Franklin about the jugglers, and Franklin is serious for the first time.

beats.scene: Rachel and Franklin laugh together in the garden beside the roses
beats.summary: Franklin and Rachel quickly become friends and spend happy days together.

beats.scene: Franklin shows a sketch of a flowery pattern to Penelope
beats.summary: Franklin loves painting and decides to decorate the door of Rachel's sitting-room as a surprise.

beats.scene: Franklin paints a pattern on a door while Penelope holds the paint pot
beats.summary: Franklin and Penelope paint the door for a whole afternoon, and in the evening one corner is still wet.

beats.scene: An old painted Indian cabinet with small drawers stands in a sunny room
beats.summary: Rachel's sitting-room has a small painted Indian cabinet where she keeps her treasures.

beats.scene: A carriage full of cheerful visitors arrives at the front door
beats.summary: Godfrey Ablewhite and his family arrive for the birthday.

beats.scene: Two young men ride off along a country road in the morning sun
beats.summary: On the birthday morning, Franklin and Godfrey ride to Frizinghall to fetch the diamond from the bank.

beats.scene: The two riders return and Franklin hands a small package to Lady Verinder
beats.summary: The riders come back with the diamond, and the whole family gathers to see it.

beats.scene: Rachel gasps as Franklin presents the glowing yellow diamond to her
beats.summary: Franklin presents the Moonstone to Rachel, and she is amazed by its beauty.

beats.scene: Rachel pins the diamond to her white dress before a looking glass
beats.summary: Rachel pins the diamond to her dress, while Lady Verinder looks on with a worried face.

beats.scene: Rachel descends the grand staircase with the diamond shining on her dress
beats.summary: That evening Rachel comes down to dinner with the diamond shining on her dress.

beats.scene: Guests in evening dress sit at a long candlelit table
beats.summary: The guests sit down to the birthday dinner, and the table shines with silver and candles.

beats.scene: Rachel sits at the table with the diamond shining on her dress
beats.summary: Rachel is the centre of the table, and the diamond draws every eye.

beats.scene: A lady leans forward to ask about the old Colonel
beats.summary: A lady asks how the Colonel won the diamond, and the talk turns to Seringapatam.

beats.scene: A tall brown-faced traveller in black sits quietly near the end of the table
beats.summary: Mr Murthwaite, a famous traveller who knows India well, listens quietly at the table.

beats.scene: The traveller holds the diamond up to the candlelight
beats.summary: Murthwaite looks closely at the diamond and says that he knows its history and its fame.

beats.scene: Murthwaite tells silent guests about the moon god and his guardians
beats.summary: Murthwaite tells of the Brahmin guardians, who still follow the stone after fifty years.

beats.scene: Franklin leans forward, speaking of the jugglers, while Murthwaite nods
beats.summary: Franklin tells him about the three Indians who followed him and who came to the house.

beats.scene: Mr Murthwaite speaks gravely to Lady Verinder across the table
beats.summary: Murthwaite says that the men are Brahmins of high rank who will never give up the diamond.

beats.scene: Lady Verinder looks anxiously at her daughter while a guest laughs
beats.summary: Lady Verinder is uneasy, but a guest makes a joke, and the room relaxes.

beats.scene: A small cheerful doctor smiles across the table at a tired Franklin
beats.summary: Dr Candy, the local doctor, notices that Franklin looks tired and begins to tease him.

beats.scene: Franklin shrugs and explains his bad nights to the doctor
beats.summary: Franklin says he has slept badly since he gave up smoking, and Dr Candy says it is his nerves.

beats.scene: The doctor wags a finger at Franklin across the table
beats.summary: Franklin laughs at the idea of a cure, and Dr Candy says he will make him sleep.

beats.scene: Carriages wait outside the house under a bright moon
beats.summary: The dinner ends, and the guests drive home through the moonlit night.

beats.scene: Lady Verinder speaks gently to Rachel near a staircase
beats.summary: Lady Verinder asks Rachel to put the diamond in a safe place for the night.

beats.scene: Rachel places the glowing diamond into a drawer of the painted cabinet
beats.summary: Rachel keeps the diamond in her own Indian cabinet, turns the key, and says good night.

beats.scene: An old steward and a footman walk through the dim hall carrying a lamp
beats.summary: Betteredge makes his nightly round of the doors and windows, with the footman Samuel.

beats.scene: Three still shapes in white stand on the moonlit terrace
beats.summary: On the terrace, Betteredge sees three dark shapes standing in the moonlight.

beats.scene: Betteredge and a footman run across the grass as the three figures slip away
beats.summary: Betteredge and Samuel run at them, and the three men melt calmly into the darkness.

beats.scene: Franklin carries a glass up the stairs, yawning, past the old steward
beats.summary: Franklin takes a glass of brandy and water up to bed, tired and yawning.

beats.scene: The moon shines over the quiet house and the sleeping garden
beats.summary: The house goes quiet, and the moon shines over the sleeping family and the locked cabinet.

beats.scene: Betteredge pours tea in a sunny kitchen at breakfast time
beats.summary: Next morning Betteredge sits down to breakfast, feeling that the dark night is over.

beats.scene: Penelope bursts in through the kitchen door, pale and breathless
beats.summary: Penelope bursts in and cries that the diamond has gone from Rachel's cabinet.

beats.scene: An open drawer of the painted cabinet, empty, in a sunny room
beats.summary: In the sitting-room, the cabinet stands open and the drawer is empty.

beats.scene: Rachel stands pale and still in the doorway of her bedroom
beats.summary: Rachel stands at her bedroom door, pale and strangely calm, and will not speak.

beats.scene: Lady Verinder hurries along the passage in her morning dress
beats.summary: Penelope fetches Lady Verinder, who is shocked but keeps her calm.

beats.scene: Franklin stands in his nightshirt and coat at the sitting-room door, astonished
beats.summary: Franklin arrives, astonished, and cannot believe the diamond is gone.

beats.scene: Servants whisper in the kitchen passage, glancing towards the stairs
beats.summary: The servants hear the news and whisper in the passage, and the word Indians is on every tongue.

beats.scene: Betteredge checks a bolted door and an unbroken window in the grey light
beats.summary: Betteredge finds every door still bolted and every window whole, and no sign of a thief.

beats.scene: Franklin and Betteredge talk in the hall beside a tall clock
beats.summary: Franklin suspects the Indians, but Betteredge points out that the house was locked all night.

beats.scene: A groom on a horse gallops down the drive towards the town
beats.summary: Lady Verinder sends for the police, and a groom gallops to Frizinghall.

beats.scene: A stout policeman in uniform steps down from a gig at the front door
beats.summary: Superintendent Seegrave arrives, a stout, important man who is sure he will solve the case quickly.

beats.scene: The policeman bends over the painted cabinet with a notebook
beats.summary: Seegrave examines the sitting-room and the cabinet and writes in his notebook.

beats.scene: Servants stand in a line in the hall while a constable counts them
beats.summary: Seegrave questions all the servants and orders a search of their boxes and rooms.

beats.scene: Betteredge speaks sternly to the policeman among angry housemaids
beats.summary: Betteredge tells the superintendent that the house servants have served the family faithfully for years.

beats.scene: A pale maid in a plain dress stands apart in the passage
beats.summary: Seegrave notices Rosanna Spearman, who has a past, and who looks pale and ill.

beats.scene: Seegrave knocks at Rachel's bedroom door, which stays shut
beats.summary: Rachel refuses to see Seegrave, and he leaves with his questions unanswered.

beats.scene: Two constables ride off down the lane after a quick word from the policeman
beats.summary: Seegrave decides that the Indian jugglers are the thieves and sends men to Frizinghall to arrest them.

beats.scene: Three calm men in white robes stand before a magistrate in a court
beats.summary: The three Indians stand calmly before the magistrate and answer politely, with nothing to hide.

beats.scene: The magistrate sends the Indians away while the policeman looks embarrassed
beats.summary: The magistrate sets the three Indians free, because nothing proves they were at the house that night.

beats.scene: Franklin speaks earnestly to Betteredge beside a library table
beats.summary: Franklin says that Seegrave is useless and that a cleverer detective must be found.

beats.scene: Franklin hands a sealed letter to a groom beside a waiting horse
beats.summary: Franklin sends a letter to Mr Bruff in London, asking him to send Sergeant Cuff.

beats.scene: Franklin points at a long smear on the wet-painted door
beats.summary: Franklin finds a smear across the painted door and sees that the wet paint was touched in the night.

beats.scene: Penelope and Betteredge look at the smeared door while a maid listens
beats.summary: Penelope says the paint was wet at midnight, and now they know when the mark was made.

beats.scene: Servants huddle in the kitchen, talking softly, while the cook shakes her head
beats.summary: The household is uneasy, and each servant wonders if the others are honest.

beats.scene: Franklin knocks at Rachel's door and waits in the passage
beats.summary: Franklin tries to talk to Rachel, but she will not see him, and he is hurt.

beats.scene: A thin grey man steps from a carriage with a small bag
beats.summary: Sergeant Cuff arrives from London, a thin, grey, elderly man in a plain black coat.

beats.scene: Sergeant Cuff bends over a rose bush, smelling a flower
beats.summary: Cuff refuses to look at the house until he has seen the roses in the garden.

beats.scene: Cuff and the old gardener argue over a white rose in a garden bed
beats.summary: Cuff and the gardener Mr Begbie argue about how to grow white moss roses.

beats.scene: Cuff walks slowly through the sitting-room, studying the floor
beats.summary: Cuff goes to the sitting-room and quietly dismisses Seegrave, who leaves in a huff.

beats.scene: Cuff looks out of the window at the empty gravel while Betteredge waits
beats.summary: Cuff says it was not the Indians, and that the thief was someone in the house.

beats.scene: Cuff holds a small glass against the smeared paint on the door
beats.summary: Cuff studies the smear on the door with a small magnifying glass.

beats.scene: Cuff points at the smear and traces a sleeve in the air
beats.summary: Cuff decides that the smear was made by a nightgown brushing against the wet paint.

beats.scene: Cuff asks Lady Verinder a question while she sits at her writing desk
beats.summary: Cuff asks Lady Verinder for leave to look at the clothes in every bedroom.

beats.scene: A pile of washing-books lies open on a table while Cuff reads
beats.summary: Cuff reads the washing-books to see which nightgowns each person owns.

beats.scene: Cuff counts the garments laid out in a bedroom and writes down a number
beats.summary: Cuff finds one nightgown missing from the count, so its owner must have hidden it.

beats.scene: A maid hurries upstairs with a bundle held tightly against her chest
beats.summary: Penelope says Rosanna shut herself in her room and has been sewing a parcel of new cloth.

beats.scene: Cuff and Betteredge walk along a shingle shore beside dark water
beats.summary: Cuff and Betteredge walk to the shore, and Cuff asks about the Shivering Sand.

beats.scene: In the distance a thin figure on a rock above the sand looks back
beats.summary: They see Rosanna in the distance as she hurries away from the sand, looking afraid.

beats.scene: Cuff looks thoughtfully at the shining sand and the grey sea
beats.summary: Cuff says that the girl has a secret and the sand is part of it.

beats.scene: A fisherman's cottage with a girl in the doorway beside nets
beats.summary: Betteredge says that Rosanna visits the fisherman's daughter Lucy Yolland, and Cuff wishes to talk to her.

beats.scene: Cuff speaks politely to Lady Verinder in a drawing-room
beats.summary: Cuff asks Lady Verinder to let him question Rachel, and she agrees.

beats.scene: Rachel stands stiffly before the detective with her hands clasped
beats.summary: Rachel enters the drawing-room, pale and proud, and answers Cuff coldly.

beats.scene: Cuff leans forward gently while Rachel looks away from him
beats.summary: Cuff asks about the cabinet, the key and the night, but Rachel gives no real help.

beats.scene: Rachel walks away down the passage, and Cuff watches her go
beats.summary: Rachel leaves the room, and Cuff says that she knows more than she tells.

beats.scene: Cuff explains his idea in a low voice to Betteredge in the hall
beats.summary: Cuff tells Betteredge his idea that Rachel hid the diamond herself, to pay a secret debt.

beats.scene: Betteredge shakes his fist at the detective in the passage
beats.summary: Betteredge is angry and says that Cuff is mad to think such a thing of Rachel.

beats.scene: Lady Verinder stands with blazing eyes as Cuff bows politely
beats.summary: Lady Verinder hears Cuff's idea and is furious that anyone should suspect her daughter.

beats.scene: Cuff lifts his hat politely at the door of the great house
beats.summary: Lady Verinder dismisses Cuff, and he leaves with a polite bow.

beats.scene: Cuff speaks quietly to Betteredge at the gate, with roses behind them
beats.summary: Cuff warns Betteredge that Rosanna will disappear and that the diamond will be found in time.

beats.scene: An untouched bed in a small maid's room with the door open
beats.summary: The next day Rosanna's room is empty and she has left the house without a word.

beats.scene: Betteredge and Franklin follow small footprints across damp sand
beats.summary: Betteredge and Franklin search the shore and find a girl's footprints leading to the Shivering Sand.

beats.scene: Fishermen stand on the shore in grey light, caps in hand
beats.summary: The news comes that Rosanna has drowned in the Shivering Sand.

beats.scene: Betteredge sits alone at a kitchen table with his old book unopened
beats.summary: Betteredge grieves for Rosanna and wonders whether he could have done more.

beats.scene: Lady Verinder and Rachel climb into a closed carriage in the drive
beats.summary: Lady Verinder takes Rachel away from the house to London, because Rachel cannot bear to stay.

beats.scene: A thin lame girl in a shawl stands at the gate with blazing eyes
beats.summary: Lucy Yolland, Rosanna's lame friend, comes to the house in great anger and asks for Franklin.

beats.scene: Franklin faces Lucy on the shingle beach as the wind blows her shawl
beats.summary: Franklin meets Lucy on the shore, and she says he broke Rosanna's heart without knowing.

beats.scene: Lucy hands a thick folded letter to Franklin with a trembling hand
beats.summary: Lucy gives Franklin a letter from Rosanna, which tells him where she hid something in the sand.

beats.scene: Franklin and Betteredge crouch on a rock and pull on a rusty chain
beats.summary: Following the letter, Franklin and Betteredge pull a chain from the rock and draw up a tin box.

beats.scene: Franklin opens a tin box and lifts out a stained white nightgown
beats.summary: Inside the box is a nightgown with a stain of paint, and Franklin's name sewn in it.

beats.scene: Franklin stares at the stained gown in his shaking hands
beats.summary: Franklin cannot understand it, decides to go to London, and Betteredge's part ends.

beats.scene: A thin woman in a plain bonnet sits at a desk covered with leaflets
beats.summary: A new writer, Miss Clack, Rachel's pious cousin, takes up the story of the diamond.

beats.scene: Miss Clack hands a leaflet to a startled butler at a front door
beats.summary: Miss Clack gives out religious leaflets to everyone she meets, whether they want them or not.

beats.scene: A tall London house stands behind iron railings in a quiet square
beats.summary: Lady Verinder takes a house in Montagu Square in London, and Miss Clack visits often.

beats.scene: A handsome smiling man speaks to a crowded hall from a platform
beats.summary: Miss Clack greatly admires her cousin Godfrey Ablewhite, a famous speaker for good causes.

beats.scene: Godfrey sits kindly beside an invalid lady, holding her hand
beats.summary: Godfrey visits Montagu Square often and is gentle and helpful to Lady Verinder and Rachel.

beats.scene: Rachel sits in a window seat, looking at a ring on her finger
beats.summary: Rachel surprises everyone by agreeing to marry Godfrey Ablewhite.

beats.scene: Lady Verinder frowns at a letter beside her daughter, who looks away
beats.summary: Lady Verinder is worried about the engagement, but Rachel has made up her mind.

beats.scene: A dry grey lawyer reads a paper at a desk piled with documents
beats.summary: Mr Bruff, the family lawyer, thinks that Godfrey's charm hides something.

beats.scene: A traveller in a dusty coat stands at the door of a London house
beats.summary: Franklin returns to London, hears that Rachel is engaged, and goes to Montagu Square.

beats.scene: Franklin stands in the drawing-room, demanding to see Rachel
beats.summary: Franklin demands to see Rachel, saying that he must know why she has turned against him.

beats.scene: Rachel enters the drawing-room and stops, pale, at the sight of Franklin
beats.summary: After many minutes Rachel comes down, and Franklin asks her what he has done.

beats.scene: Rachel points an accusing finger at Franklin in a lamplit room
beats.summary: Rachel tells Franklin that she saw him take the diamond from her cabinet with her own eyes.

beats.scene: Franklin shakes his head slowly, white-faced, as Rachel turns away
beats.summary: Franklin cannot believe it, saying that he remembers nothing of the kind.

beats.scene: Rachel clasps her hands tightly as she speaks, her eyes bright with tears
beats.summary: Rachel says she kept silent to protect him, because she loved him.

beats.scene: Franklin lays a stained nightgown on a table before Rachel
beats.summary: Franklin tells Rachel about the stained gown with his name, but she gives no answer.

beats.scene: A nurse and a doctor stand by the bed of Lady Verinder
beats.summary: Soon afterwards Lady Verinder becomes ill, and the doctors say that there is little hope.

beats.scene: Rachel kneels beside a still bed, her head on her mother's hand
beats.summary: Lady Verinder dies, and Rachel is heartbroken.

beats.scene: Mr Bruff reads aloud from a will to Rachel and Godfrey in the library
beats.summary: Mr Bruff reads the will, which puts Rachel's money in a trust so that she only receives the income.

beats.scene: Godfrey rises from a chair with a stiff smile and picks up his hat
beats.summary: Godfrey hears that he cannot touch Rachel's money, and his charm cracks for a moment.

beats.scene: Godfrey writes a letter at his desk, pausing with a pen
beats.summary: Godfrey writes to break off the engagement, and Rachel is left alone, with no one to trust.

beats.scene: Franklin sits alone at a desk by a lamp, pen in hand
beats.summary: A year later Franklin takes up the story himself, still hoping to clear his name.

beats.scene: A carriage rolls along a green Yorkshire lane towards a grey house
beats.summary: Franklin returns to Yorkshire and goes to the old house to see Betteredge again.

beats.scene: Betteredge and Franklin talk across a kitchen table over cups of tea
beats.summary: Betteredge tells Franklin the news: Seegrave is forgotten, Cuff is gone, and Dr Candy is ill.

beats.scene: Franklin walks up the path to a small doctor's house with a brass plate
beats.summary: Franklin calls at Dr Candy's house, hoping that the doctor can remember something.

beats.scene: A tall thin man with black and white hair stands in a doorway
beats.summary: Franklin meets Ezra Jennings, the doctor's assistant, who has strange hair, black in some places and white in others.

beats.scene: Villagers turn their backs on Ezra Jennings in the street
beats.summary: Betteredge says that the village does not like Ezra, and nobody knows where he came from.

beats.scene: Ezra sits in a quiet room, holding a small bottle and looking tired
beats.summary: Ezra tells Franklin that he is a sick man and takes medicine every day for his pain.

beats.scene: Franklin and Ezra walk slowly across a hillside, talking
beats.summary: Franklin and Ezra walk together, and Franklin tells him the strange story of the diamond.

beats.scene: Ezra pulls a little notebook from his coat and looks at Franklin carefully
beats.summary: Ezra says he wrote down the odd words Dr Candy spoke in his fever, and thinks they may matter.

beats.scene: Franklin holds a page of scrawled notes in the evening light
beats.summary: Franklin reads the broken words, and they seem to hint at a secret about that night.

beats.scene: Ezra puts the broken notes in order at a table
beats.summary: Ezra fills in the gaps in Dr Candy's muddled words and finds the meaning.

beats.scene: Ezra speaks earnestly to Franklin in a small room with books
beats.summary: Ezra explains that Dr Candy secretly gave Franklin laudanum on the night of the birthday.

beats.scene: Franklin stares in shock at Ezra with his hand on a chair
beats.summary: Franklin remembers the glass he drank and cannot speak for a moment.

beats.scene: A page from a medical book lies open on the table, with a pen
beats.summary: Ezra explains that laudanum can make a nervous man move and act in his sleep.

beats.scene: Franklin walks up and down the room, thinking hard
beats.summary: Franklin realises that he may have taken the diamond himself while drugged.

beats.scene: Franklin speaks warmly to Ezra, taking his hands
beats.summary: Franklin guesses that he was worried about the diamond and took it to keep it safe.

beats.scene: Ezra draws a plan on paper while Franklin leans over the table
beats.summary: Ezra suggests that they repeat the night exactly, with the same dose, to see what Franklin does.

beats.scene: Franklin writes a letter to a lawyer in a London office
beats.summary: Franklin knows he needs a witness, and he writes to Mr Bruff to ask for help.

beats.scene: Mr Bruff listens, frowning, to Ezra at the table in a country inn
beats.summary: Mr Bruff arrives in Yorkshire, listens to Ezra's reasons and agrees to help.

beats.scene: Franklin writes to Rachel at a desk beside a window
beats.summary: Franklin writes to Rachel to tell her about the plan and begs her to come and see the experiment.

beats.scene: Rachel reads a letter beside a window in a London room
beats.summary: Rachel reads Franklin's letter by the window in Montagu Square with trembling hands.

beats.scene: Rachel writes a short reply at a small table, with tears on the paper
beats.summary: Rachel replies with a few lines: she will come to Yorkshire and watch.

beats.scene: Betteredge and Franklin carry a chair through the empty sitting-room
beats.summary: The sitting-room is put back as it was on the night of the birthday, and Betteredge helps.

beats.scene: Franklin throws a box of cigars into a fire while Betteredge laughs
beats.summary: Franklin gives up smoking again so that he will sleep as badly as he did that summer.

beats.scene: Rachel steps from a carriage at dusk with a veil over her face
beats.summary: Rachel arrives quietly on the evening of the experiment, and she is hidden away.

beats.scene: Ezra measures a few drops into a glass of brandy and water
beats.summary: Ezra measures out the dose, the same as Dr Candy gave, and Franklin drinks it.

beats.scene: Two men sit in the dark passage outside a closed bedroom door
beats.summary: Ezra and Mr Bruff sit in the dark passage, watching and waiting for hours.

beats.scene: A bedroom door opens slowly in the dark and a pale figure appears
beats.summary: Franklin, drugged, rises from his bed and opens his door, with a fixed and glassy look.

beats.scene: Franklin walks through a dark house in his nightclothes
beats.summary: Franklin walks along the dark passages of the house towards Rachel's sitting-room, with the watchers following.

beats.scene: Franklin opens a drawer of the cabinet and lifts out a glass gem
beats.summary: Franklin enters the sitting-room and takes the false diamond from the drawer, with Rachel watching in tears.

beats.scene: Franklin walks back along the dark passage holding the glass stone
beats.summary: Franklin carries the false diamond back to his own room, and the watchers follow quietly.

beats.scene: Mr Bruff and Ezra shake hands in the passage in the first grey light
beats.summary: Ezra and Mr Bruff agree that the experiment has proved that Franklin acted in his sleep.

beats.scene: Rachel steps out of the shadows into the pale light of the sitting-room
beats.summary: Rachel comes out of her hiding-place, and she knows now that she had been wrong about Franklin.

beats.scene: Franklin wakes in bed and sees Rachel bending over him
beats.summary: Franklin wakes at sunrise, confused, and finds Rachel at his bedside.

beats.scene: Rachel and Franklin embrace beside the window in the pink dawn
beats.summary: Rachel begs Franklin to forgive her, and he says there is nothing to forgive.

beats.scene: Rachel holds the stained nightgown, her face soft with sorrow
beats.summary: They understand that Rosanna hid the stained gown because she loved Franklin and wished to protect him.

beats.scene: Franklin stands in the empty sitting-room looking at the open drawer
beats.summary: Franklin points out that the real diamond is still missing, and asks who took it from his room.

beats.scene: Mr Bruff taps his chin and speaks to the three young people
beats.summary: Mr Bruff says the thief is someone who knew that Franklin carried the stone, and that Cuff is needed.

beats.scene: Cuff trims a rose with a small knife in a cottage garden
beats.summary: Sergeant Cuff has retired to grow roses at Dorking, and Mr Bruff writes to him.

beats.scene: Cuff steps off a train with a small bag and a rose
beats.summary: Cuff arrives, and he is curious and pleased to find that Rachel's secret is at last cleared up.

beats.scene: Cuff sits in an armchair, tapping his fingertips together as he thinks
beats.summary: Cuff asks who else was in the house that night, and who might have seen Franklin walking.

beats.scene: Mr Bruff leans forward with a thoughtful frown at the library table
beats.summary: Mr Bruff remembers Godfrey's face when he heard the will, and Cuff asks about Godfrey's money.

beats.scene: A grey man speaks to a street clerk in a doorway
beats.summary: Cuff sets his helpers to ask questions in London, and he learns that Godfrey has a secret second house.

beats.scene: A worried gentleman counts coins and bills at a desk piled with papers
beats.summary: Cuff learns that Godfrey spent money that did not belong to him and owed it back by a certain day.

beats.scene: Cuff explains his idea to Franklin and Mr Bruff around a table
beats.summary: Cuff explains that Godfrey, awake that night, saw Franklin walk with the stone and took it from him.

beats.scene: A pawnbroker's shop door with three brass balls in a narrow street
beats.summary: Cuff says a diamond cannot be sold easily, so Godfrey must have borrowed money against it from Mr Luker.

beats.scene: A boy in a large hat watches a gate from behind a lamp-post
beats.summary: Cuff sets his boy Gooseberry to watch Mr Luker's house, and Gooseberry soon reports back.

beats.scene: A fat moneylender hurries to a bank with a small parcel under his arm
beats.summary: Gooseberry sees Luker take a small packet to his bank in Lombard Street.

beats.scene: Cuff, Mr Bruff and Gooseberry watch a bank doorway from across a busy street
beats.summary: On the day the loan is due, Cuff and his men watch the bank in Lombard Street.

beats.scene: Godfrey hands money across a counter and receives a small packet
beats.summary: Godfrey comes, pays Mr Luker, and takes the packet from the bank.

beats.scene: A man in a rough sailor's coat hurries along a London street, looking back
beats.summary: Godfrey leaves the bank in a hurry, afraid, and Gooseberry follows him through the crowd.

beats.scene: A guest signs his name in the book of a quiet old London inn
beats.summary: Godfrey, afraid, hides in an old inn called Tolliver's under a false name.

beats.scene: Three silent men in white robes enter a dark room by lamplight
beats.summary: During the night the three Indians, who have followed Godfrey, slip into his room.

beats.scene: A candle burns beside an empty bed in a small inn room
beats.summary: In the morning Godfrey is found dead in his room, and the diamond has gone.

beats.scene: Cuff and Mr Bruff stand silently beside a bed in the inn
beats.summary: Cuff and Mr Bruff are called to the inn, and they recognise Godfrey Ablewhite despite his false name.

beats.scene: Cuff explains in a quiet room while the others listen with bowed heads
beats.summary: Cuff explains that the Indians had done only what their oath demanded, and they sail from England.

beats.scene: Franklin and Rachel stand hand in hand in the doorway of a village church
beats.summary: Franklin and Rachel marry, and old Betteredge is delighted at the wedding.

beats.scene: A letter from Mr Murthwaite lies on a table in candlelight
beats.summary: Mr Murthwaite writes from India that he has seen three Indian priests at a great festival, and the stone is not far away.

beats.scene: A great crowd gathers at night in front of a temple on the hill
beats.summary: The pilgrims carry the stone in a procession to the holy city of Somnauth, where it is returned to the moon god.

beats.scene: A glowing yellow diamond shines in the forehead of the moon god statue
beats.summary: The diamond shines again in the forehead of the moon god, back where its long story began.

A1A2: In India, a large yellow diamond shone in the forehead of a god.
Three priests promised to guard the diamond for all of their lives.
An old story said that thieves of the diamond would meet bad luck.
Many years later, the diamond was kept inside a strong fortress.
In 1799, English soldiers attacked the fortress of Seringapatam.
A young officer named John Herncastle went to look for the diamond.
He found the room and took the diamond for himself.
Herncastle went home to England, but his friends kept away.
The Colonel lived alone in London, and he was always afraid.
When the Colonel died, he left the diamond to his niece Rachel.
Gabriel Betteredge is an old man, and he sits down to write.
Betteredge loves one book, and its name is Robinson Crusoe.
The Verinder house stands in Yorkshire, close to the sea.
Lady Verinder is a kind woman, and she is also very wise.
Her daughter Rachel is proud, but she is also very kind.
Betteredge's daughter Penelope works as Rachel's maid and tells him everything.
One maid, Rosanna Spearman, used to steal things.
Rosanna was plain and shy, and she had few friends.
Near the house there was a dangerous place called the Shivering Sand.
Rosanna often went there alone and sat for hours.
A letter came to say that Franklin Blake was coming.
Franklin had lived in many countries, and he was clever and kind.
Franklin was going to bring the diamond with him from London.
One afternoon, three Indian men came to the door.
The men threw bright balls high into the air.
The leader asked if an English gentleman was coming to the house.
Betteredge sent them away, but he did not feel happy.
Franklin Blake arrived at the house on a hot afternoon.
Franklin said that some Indian men had followed him there.
Betteredge told him about the three men at the door.
Franklin and Rachel liked each other, and they laughed a lot.
Franklin loved to paint, and he had a plan for Rachel's door.
Franklin and Penelope painted the door for many hours.
Rachel's room had a small painted cabinet with a lock.
Godfrey Ablewhite and his family came for the birthday.
On the birthday morning, the two men rode to town.
At noon, the men came back with the precious diamond.
Rachel gasped when she saw the great yellow diamond.
Rachel pinned the diamond to her dress, and she looked happy.
That evening, Rachel came down to dinner with the diamond shining.
Twenty guests sat down at a long table full of candles.
Rachel sat in the middle, and everyone looked at her diamond.
A lady asked how the Colonel got the diamond.
A tall traveller named Murthwaite sat quietly at the table.
Murthwaite looked closely at the diamond and said he knew it.
He said three priests still followed the stone, after fifty years.
Franklin told him about the three men who followed him.
Murthwaite said these men would never give up their search.
Lady Verinder looked worried, but a guest made a joke.
Dr Candy saw that Franklin looked very tired.
Franklin said he had slept badly since he stopped smoking.
Franklin laughed, and the doctor said he could cure it.
After dinner, the guests drove away in the moonlight.
Lady Verinder asked Rachel to put the diamond away safely.
Rachel locked the diamond in a drawer and said good night.
Betteredge walked around the house to lock every door.
On the terrace, he saw three dark shapes in the moonlight.
Betteredge shouted and ran, but the men were gone.
Franklin took a drink upstairs and went to bed.
The house became quiet, and the moon shone on the roof.
The next morning, Betteredge sat down to his breakfast.
Penelope ran in and cried, “The diamond is gone!”
In the cabinet, the little drawer was open and empty.
Rachel stood at her bedroom door, pale and silent.
Penelope called Lady Verinder, who came quickly to the room.
Franklin came in and could not believe his eyes.
The servants heard the news and began to talk fast.
Every door was locked, and every window was still whole.
Franklin blamed the Indians, but the house had been locked.
Lady Verinder sent for the police, and a groom rode fast.
Superintendent Seegrave arrived and said he would soon find the thief.
He looked at the cabinet and wrote in his notebook.
He wanted to search the rooms of all the servants.
Betteredge said the servants had worked there for many years.
Seegrave saw Rosanna, who looked pale and was not well.
Seegrave knocked on Rachel's door, but she did not answer.
Seegrave decided that the Indians were the thieves.
The three men stood calmly in front of the judge.
The judge freed the three men, and Seegrave looked foolish.
Franklin said they needed a much cleverer detective than Seegrave.
Franklin wrote to his lawyer and asked for Sergeant Cuff.
Franklin found a long smear across the painted door.
Penelope said the paint was still wet at midnight.
The servants were afraid, and nobody trusted anybody.
Franklin tried to speak to Rachel, but she would not see him.
Sergeant Cuff arrived, a thin grey man in black.
First, Cuff wanted to see the roses in the garden.
Cuff argued with the gardener about how to grow roses.
At last Cuff went to the room where the cabinet stood.
Cuff said the thief was someone inside the house.
Cuff looked at the smear with a small glass.
Cuff said someone's clothes had touched the wet paint at night.
Cuff asked to look at the night clothes of everyone in the house.
Cuff read the washing books to see who owned what.
Cuff found that one set of night clothes was missing.
Penelope said Rosanna had been sewing alone in her room.
Cuff and Betteredge walked along the shore together.
They saw Rosanna hurry away from the sand, looking afraid.
Cuff said that the girl had a secret and the sand knew it.
Rosanna's friend Lucy Yolland lived in a fisherman's cottage nearby.
Cuff asked to speak to Rachel, and her mother agreed.
Rachel came into the room, pale and proud and cold.
Cuff asked about the key, but Rachel said very little.
When Rachel left, Cuff said she knew more than she said.
Cuff thought that Rachel had hidden the diamond herself.
Betteredge was angry and said that Cuff was mad.
Lady Verinder heard his idea and was very angry.
Lady Verinder asked Cuff to leave the case and the house.
Cuff said Rosanna would soon leave, and he went away.
The next day, Rosanna's room was empty, and she was gone.
They found small footprints leading across the damp sand.
Sad news came that Rosanna had died in the Shivering Sand.
Betteredge was very sad, and he asked himself questions.
Lady Verinder took Rachel to London in a closed carriage.
Lucy Yolland came to the house and asked for Franklin.
Lucy told Franklin that he had broken Rosanna's heart.
Lucy gave him a letter that told of a hiding place.
They pulled a chain, and a small tin box came up.
Inside the box was a white night shirt with Franklin's name on it.
Franklin did not understand, so he left for London that night.
Now Miss Clack, Rachel's cousin, began to tell the story.
Miss Clack gave a little book about God to everyone she met.
Lady Verinder's London house was in Montagu Square.
Miss Clack greatly admired her cousin Godfrey, a speaker.
Godfrey visited often and was kind to Rachel and her mother.
To everyone's surprise, Rachel agreed to marry Godfrey.
Lady Verinder was worried, but Rachel had made her choice.
Mr Bruff, the family lawyer, was not sure about Godfrey.
Franklin came back to London and went to Montagu Square.
Franklin said he must see Rachel and learn the truth.
Rachel came down, and Franklin asked her what he had done.
Rachel said, “I saw you take the diamond myself.”
Franklin said he remembered nothing and could not believe it.
Rachel said she kept quiet because she had loved him.
Franklin told Rachel about the night shirt, but she said nothing.
Soon after that, Lady Verinder became very ill.
Lady Verinder died, and Rachel was heartbroken.
The will placed Rachel's money in the care of trustees.
Godfrey heard the news and his smile became very stiff.
Godfrey ended the engagement, and Rachel was left alone.
A year later, Franklin wrote his own part of the story.
Franklin went back to Yorkshire to see old Betteredge.
Betteredge told him the news, and Dr Candy was ill.
Franklin went to Dr Candy's house to ask him questions.
Ezra Jennings had hair that was black and white together.
Ezra was new to the village, and people did not like him.
Ezra said he was a sick man and took medicine.
They walked together, and Franklin told him the whole story.
Ezra said that he had written down the doctor's fever words.
Franklin read the broken words, and they were very strange.
Ezra put the broken words in order and found a meaning.
Ezra said Dr Candy had put sleep medicine in Franklin's drink.
Franklin remembered the glass and could not speak.
Ezra said the drug could make a man act in his sleep.
Franklin realised that he might have taken the diamond himself.
Franklin thought he took it only to keep it safe.
Ezra said they should repeat that night exactly, to see.
Franklin wrote to Mr Bruff, because he needed a witness.
Mr Bruff came to Yorkshire and agreed to help.
Franklin wrote to Rachel, and he told her the plan.
Rachel read the letter by the window with shaking hands.
Rachel replied that she would come and watch the experiment.
Betteredge helped them put back the room, with a false stone.
Franklin stopped smoking again, so that he would sleep badly.
Rachel arrived quietly in the evening, and she hid.
Ezra measured the dose, and Franklin drank the glass.
Ezra and Mr Bruff waited in the dark passage.
In the night, Franklin got up and opened the door.
Franklin walked slowly through the dark house toward the sitting-room.
Franklin took the false diamond from the drawer, and Rachel cried.
Franklin carried the false stone back to his own room.
Mr Bruff and Ezra agreed that the experiment was proved.
Rachel came out of her hiding place, and she knew.
Franklin woke and saw Rachel standing beside his bed.
Rachel asked him to forgive her, and they embraced.
They understood that Rosanna had hidden the gown to protect him.
But the real diamond was still missing, and nobody knew where.
Mr Bruff said that they needed a clever detective.
Cuff had retired to grow roses in a place called Dorking.
Cuff came to hear the story, and he looked pleased.
Cuff asked who else was in the house that night.
Mr Bruff remembered how Godfrey had looked at the will.
Cuff found out that Godfrey had a secret house in Northwood.
Godfrey owed a lot of money and had very little.
Cuff said Godfrey saw Franklin walk and took the stone.
Cuff said Godfrey borrowed money from Mr Luker, a man who lends money.
A boy named Gooseberry watched Luker's house for Cuff.
Luker took a small packet to his bank in Lombard Street.
On the day, Cuff's men watched the bank in Lombard Street.
Godfrey came, paid the money, and took the packet away.
Godfrey hurried away in fear, and Gooseberry followed him.
Godfrey hid in a quiet inn under a false name.
In the night, three men in white came to his room.
In the morning, Godfrey was found dead, and the diamond was gone.
Cuff and Mr Bruff came and knew the dead man.
Cuff said the three men had only kept their oath.
Franklin and Rachel married, and Betteredge was very happy.
Mr Murthwaite wrote from India about the three priests.
The stone was carried to the holy city of Somnauth.
Once more, the diamond shone in the moon god's forehead.
B1B2: Long ago, in a temple in India, a huge yellow diamond shone from the forehead of a statue of the moon god. People said that its light grew brighter and weaker as the moon grew full and thin.
Three Brahmin priests were chosen to guard the stone, and each swore a sacred oath over the statue. When they grew old, their sons took their places, so that the watch never ended.

An old legend warned that anyone who took the diamond by force would bring disaster on himself and his family. The priests believed this completely, and they told the story to every visitor who came near the stone.

Over the centuries, wars and conquerors moved the diamond from place to place. By 1799 it lay in the fortress of Seringapatam, which was ruled by Tipu Sultan, and the three priests were never far away.

In May 1799 the English army attacked Seringapatam, and after a short, fierce fight its soldiers broke through the walls. The fortress fell in a single afternoon, and the streets filled with smoke and noise.
Among the English officers was a young man named John Herncastle, who had heard stories of the famous diamond. While the others fought in the streets, he went quietly to look for it.
Herncastle reached the room where the stone was kept, and he took it for himself. When the night was over, some men lay dead, and nobody could say exactly what had happened.

Herncastle returned to England with the diamond hidden among his belongings, and people soon began to whisper about him. His friends turned away, and even his own sister, Lady Verinder, would not receive him.
For many years the Colonel lived alone in London behind locked doors, and he seldom went out. People said that he was afraid of three Indian men who were always somewhere in the streets.
When the Colonel died in 1848, his will left the diamond to Rachel Verinder on her eighteenth birthday. Her mother, who had never forgiven her brother, suspected that it was meant as a cruel joke.
Gabriel Betteredge, the old steward of Lady Verinder's house, has been asked to write down all he remembers about the diamond. He lights his pipe, opens a clean book and begins at the beginning.
Betteredge trusts one book above all others, and it is Robinson Crusoe. Whenever he is worried, he opens it at random, and he always finds the advice that he needs.

Lady Verinder's large house stands in Yorkshire, not far from the sea, with fields on one side and sand hills on the other. Betteredge has worked there for nearly fifty years, and he knows every room and every secret.
Lady Verinder is a widow, and she has been calm and sensible ever since her husband died. She is kind to everyone who works for her, and she hates a quarrel more than anything.
Rachel is the only daughter of the house, and she will be eighteen in June. She is proud and quick, with a mind of her own, but she is generous to the servants and always speaks the truth.

Betteredge's daughter Penelope is Rachel's maid, and she is quick, cheerful and very good at finding things out. Every evening she tells her father everything that has been said upstairs, whether he asks for it or not.
One of the housemaids, Rosanna Spearman, was once a thief and spent time in a reformatory. Lady Verinder, who believed in second chances, brought her to the house to begin a better life.
Rosanna was thin and plain, and one of her shoulders was higher than the other. She worked hard and kept to herself, and the other maids could not understand her quiet ways.

Not far from the house, between two rocky points, lay a dangerous quicksand known as the Shivering Sand. When the tide turned, its surface trembled and shook, and it was said to swallow anything that touched it.

In her free hours Rosanna often walked to the Shivering Sand and sat on a rock above it, looking down at the sand. Betteredge scolded her gently for it, but she only said that the place seemed to draw her.
One morning a letter arrived at the house to say that Franklin Blake was coming to stay. Betteredge remembered him as a clever, lively boy, and he was delighted by the news.

Franklin had spent his life abroad, studying in France, Germany and Italy, and he seemed to have three or four characters at once. Betteredge said that he could be gay, serious or dreamy, depending on which country he had last remembered.
The family soon learned that Franklin would bring the Colonel's diamond for Rachel's birthday. Lady Verinder was worried by the thought, but Rachel was as excited as any girl of seventeen would be.
One afternoon Penelope ran to find her father, because three Indian men in white clothes were standing at the front door. They had a small English boy with them, and they said they were jugglers.

Before Betteredge could stop them, the men began to throw bright brass balls high into the air and to catch them behind their backs. The servants gathered at the windows and clapped, and Penelope stood laughing in the doorway.

When the show ended, the leader poured a little ink into the English boy's hand and asked him to look into it. Then, in careful English, he asked whether a gentleman from foreign parts was expected at the house.

Betteredge sent the men away at once and warned them that he would call the police if they came back. They bowed politely and left, but he could not forget their calm faces, and he felt uneasy for the rest of the day.
Franklin arrived the next day in a hired carriage, cheerful, dusty and a little tired from the journey. Betteredge was so glad to see him that he almost forgot to be formal.

Franklin said that he had left the diamond in a bank in Frizinghall, because he thought it would be safer there. He also admitted that he had noticed some Indian men following him from London, and he wondered why.
That evening Betteredge told Franklin about the jugglers and the question about a gentleman from foreign parts. For the first time since his arrival, the young man grew quiet and serious.

In the days that followed, Franklin and Rachel became close friends, and they were soon laughing and teasing each other all day long. Betteredge, who watched them closely, began to wonder whether the friendship might become something more.
Franklin was fond of painting, and he decided to decorate the door of Rachel's little sitting-room as a birthday surprise. He asked Penelope to help him, and she agreed at once.
Franklin and Penelope worked on the door for the whole afternoon, and he mixed the paint himself. By evening the pattern was finished, but one corner of the paint was still slightly wet.

Rachel's sitting-room held a small Indian cabinet, painted in bright colours and fitted with several little drawers. It was her favourite piece of furniture, and she kept her most precious things inside it.

On the day before the birthday, Rachel's cousin Godfrey Ablewhite arrived with his family from Frizinghall. He was a tall, handsome man with a warm smile, and everyone said he was the kindest man in England.

On the morning of the birthday, Franklin and Godfrey rode together to Frizinghall to fetch the diamond from the bank. Betteredge watched them go, and he was relieved to see that nobody was following them.
At noon the two men came back, and Franklin carried a small sealed package under his coat. The family gathered in the drawing-room, and even Betteredge found an excuse to stand near the door.
The Moonstone was as large as a plover's egg, and it glowed with a deep yellow light, like captured sunshine. Rachel gasped with delight, and everyone in the room fell silent.
Rachel pinned the diamond to the front of her white dress and turned this way and that before the mirror. Her mother smiled, but Betteredge could see that Lady Verinder was thinking of the Colonel.

That evening, as the guests arrived for the birthday dinner, Rachel came down the great staircase with the diamond glowing on her dress. Every head turned, and a murmur of admiration ran through the hall.
Twenty guests sat down to the birthday dinner, and the long table shone with silver and candlelight. Betteredge walked behind the chairs, and he watched every plate and every face.
Rachel sat near the middle of the table, and the diamond blazed on her white dress whenever she moved. The guests found it hard to talk about anything else.
Between the soup and the fish, a lady asked how the Colonel had come by such a stone. Nobody at the table could give her a clear answer.
Near the end of the table sat Mr Murthwaite, a tall, quiet man who had travelled for years in the wildest parts of India. He had hardly spoken all evening, but he was listening to everything.
When Rachel held out the stone, Mr Murthwaite looked at it for a long time without speaking. At last he said that its story was famous across the whole of India.
He told the guests that the priests who guarded the stone had never given up their search. Their oath, he said, was handed from father to son, and fifty years was nothing to them.
Franklin leaned forward and told Mr Murthwaite about the three Indians who had followed him in London. He also described the jugglers who had come to the door that very week.
Mr Murthwaite said that the men were Brahmins of high rank, and that they must have given up much to cross the sea. Such men, he warned, would not stop until the diamond was theirs again.
Lady Verinder looked anxiously at her daughter, and the room grew very still. Then Godfrey Ablewhite made a cheerful joke about Indian jugglers, and everybody laughed with relief.
When the laughter had faded, small, cheerful Dr Candy noticed that Franklin looked pale and tired. He began to tease him about it, as doctors will, in front of the whole table.
Franklin admitted that he had slept very badly ever since he gave up his cigars. Dr Candy replied that this was a simple case of tired nerves.
Franklin laughed and said that doctors had never cured anybody's sleeplessness. Dr Candy answered, a little hurt, that he would make Mr Franklin sleep like a baby, and that was a promise.
When the last of the dessert had gone, the guests said their goodbyes and went out to their carriages. Mr Murthwaite shook hands with Lady Verinder and drove away through the moonlit lanes.
Lady Verinder came to Rachel on the stairs and begged her to lock the diamond in a safe place for the night. She did not like having such a stone in the house at all.
Rachel laid the diamond in one of the cabinet's little drawers and turned the key with a smile. Then she kissed her mother and said good night to Penelope.

As he did every night, Betteredge went around the house with the footman Samuel to see that every door and window was locked. Tonight he took more care than usual, because of the stories about the Indians.

When Betteredge opened the door to the terrace, he saw three figures standing perfectly still in the moonlight. Their long robes were pale against the dark grass, and they were looking up at the house.
Betteredge shouted and ran at them with Samuel behind him, but the three men turned and walked away into the shadows. By the time he reached the gate, there was nobody there at all.
Franklin, yawning widely, took a glass of brandy and water up to his bedroom. Betteredge thought nothing of it, because a tired man may take a drink before he goes to bed.
One by one the lights went out, and the great house fell silent. The moon shone down on the roof, and nobody inside heard anything more that night.
Next morning, Betteredge woke early and felt better about the Indians in the light of day. He was just sitting down to his breakfast when he heard running feet.
Penelope burst in, pale and out of breath, and cried that the diamond had gone from Miss Rachel's cabinet. She could say no more, and she held on to the table.

The Indian cabinet stood in the corner exactly as it had stood the night before, but the little drawer was open and quite empty. Betteredge looked into it twice, as if the stone might be hiding in a corner.
Rachel stood in the doorway of her bedroom, pale and strangely calm, with her eyes on the empty drawer. When Betteredge spoke to her, she did not seem to hear him.
Penelope fetched Lady Verinder, who came quickly in her morning dress and looked at the cabinet in dismay. She said nothing for some time, and then she asked quietly where Rachel was.
Franklin arrived a moment later with his coat thrown over his shoulders, and he could hardly believe what he saw. He said again and again that the diamond had been safe in the bank for a month.
Before breakfast was over, the news had run through the house from the kitchen to the stables. The servants whispered in corners, and the word Indians was on every tongue.
Betteredge went around the whole house again, and he found every bolt in place and every window unbroken. There were no footprints on the terrace, and the dew lay smooth on the grass.
Franklin said at once that the three Indians must have done it. Betteredge replied that no stranger could have entered a house that was locked up so tightly.
Lady Verinder decided that the police must be called without any delay. A groom saddled the fastest horse in the stable and galloped off to Frizinghall, and Betteredge watched him out of sight.
Superintendent Seegrave arrived at eleven o'clock, a stout man in uniform with a loud voice. He told the household that the thief would be in prison before the day was out.
Seegrave went to the sitting-room and examined the cabinet, the window and the carpet with great seriousness. He wrote in his notebook after each one, and he said, “Hm,” a good many times.
Seegrave then ordered that every servant's room and box should be searched for the stone. The maids were furious, and Penelope said that she would leave the house at once.
Betteredge told the superintendent that most of the servants had served the family for many years. He said that any search of their things would be an insult to honest people.
Seegrave soon noticed that one housemaid, Rosanna Spearman, looked pale and ill and kept apart from the others. When he heard that she had once been in prison, his eyes began to shine.
Seegrave knocked on Rachel's bedroom door and asked to see her, but she refused to open it. She sent word that she wished to see no policeman, and that she knew nothing.

Seegrave decided that the three Indian jugglers must be the thieves, since they had been seen near the house. He sent two constables to Frizinghall, and by evening the three men were in the police station.
The next day the three Indians stood before the magistrate in Frizinghall, calm and polite. They spoke good English, and they answered every question without any sign of fear.
The magistrate found that the men had been in Frizinghall at the time of the theft, and no stone was found on them. He set them free, and Seegrave went red in the face.
When Franklin heard the news, he said that Seegrave was hopeless and a cleverer man must be found. He remembered that his lawyer, Mr Bruff, knew of a famous detective in London.
Franklin wrote to Mr Bruff in London that very afternoon and begged him to send Sergeant Cuff. A groom carried the letter to the station, and for a day the house waited.
While the house waited, Franklin noticed a long smear across the pattern on Rachel's door. The paint had been wet when they went to bed, so someone must have brushed against it in the night.
Penelope remembered that the paint had been wet when she said good night to Rachel, at about midnight. That meant that the smear was made after midnight, and before the morning.
The whole house had become uneasy, and each servant wondered quietly about all the others. Even old friends spoke to one another in low voices, and the kitchen was never cheerful.
Franklin knocked at Rachel's door several times, but she would not talk to him. He had been her best friend only a week before, and now she looked at him with cold eyes.
Sergeant Cuff arrived by the afternoon train, a thin, grey, sad-looking man dressed in black. His eyes were a faded grey, and they seemed to look through the people they rested on.
Before he looked at a single clue, Sergeant Cuff asked to be shown the garden. He had heard of the old roses at the house, and he wished to see them.
Cuff and the gardener, Mr Begbie, were soon deep in an argument about white moss roses and how to grow them. Cuff said that nothing was better for a rose than a little soap and water.
At last Cuff followed Betteredge into the house and went to the sitting-room. He thanked Superintendent Seegrave politely for his work, and the superintendent left rather quickly.
Cuff stood for a long moment in silence, and then he told Betteredge that the Indians had not taken the diamond. Whoever had done this, he said gently, was someone who slept under this roof.
Sergeant Cuff took a small glass from his pocket and looked at the smear on the door for a very long time. Then he stepped back and looked at it again from the other side of the room.
At last Cuff announced that the mark had been made by a piece of cloth, and most likely by a nightgown. Whoever had brushed against the door must have a stain on that garment.
Cuff asked Lady Verinder for leave to examine the nightclothes of everybody who slept in the house. She was reluctant, but she gave her permission, because she wanted the truth.
Cuff asked for the washing-books, in which the laundry maid wrote down every garment that went to the wash. He read them page by page and checked each name against the list of nightgowns.
When he had finished, Cuff said that every nightgown was in its place, except one that had gone missing from the washing. Its owner must have hidden it, and Cuff meant to find out why.
Penelope remembered that Rosanna had been ill on the Thursday and had shut herself in her room to sew. She had also gone alone to Frizinghall that afternoon and come back with a parcel.
Cuff asked to see the Shivering Sand, so Betteredge led him down the cliff path to the shore. As they walked, the detective asked many questions about Rosanna Spearman.
Far off along the sand they saw a thin figure on the rocks, and Betteredge knew it was Rosanna. She saw them too, and she turned and hurried away with her head down.
Cuff said quietly that the girl was hiding something and that it had something to do with the sand. He added that he was not yet sure whether she had stolen the diamond herself.
Betteredge told him that Rosanna's only friend was Lucy Yolland, a fisherman's daughter who lived in a cottage nearby. Cuff said that he would like to speak to Lucy Yolland before the week was out.
Cuff told Lady Verinder that he could not go further without speaking to Rachel herself. She agreed to ask her daughter, though she was not sure that Rachel would come.
Rachel entered the drawing-room with her head held high, and she looked at Cuff as if he were a stranger. She answered his questions as briefly as she possibly could.
Cuff asked her when she had last seen the stone, and whether anyone else had a key to the cabinet. Rachel said that she had locked the diamond away herself, and she would say no more.
Rachel left the room as suddenly as she had entered it, and the door closed behind her. Cuff said, half to himself, that the young lady knew a great deal more than she was telling.

In a low voice, Cuff told Betteredge that he suspected Miss Rachel had hidden the diamond herself. Young ladies sometimes have secret debts, he explained, and a stone like that could pay a great many.
Betteredge answered in a rage that Cuff must be out of his mind to say such a thing of Miss Rachel. He had known her since she was a baby, and she had never owed a penny.
When Lady Verinder heard what Cuff thought, her face turned white with anger. She said that nobody had the right to accuse her daughter of stealing her own diamond.
Lady Verinder thanked Cuff for his time and paid him, but she told him that his help was no longer wanted. He bowed politely, put on his hat and walked out through the door.
At the gate Cuff told Betteredge to watch Rosanna Spearman, for she would soon do something strange. He added that the diamond would turn up in the end, and that his address was in London.
The next morning Rosanna Spearman was not at breakfast, and her bed had not been slept in. She had put on her hat and walked out of the house without saying a word to anyone.
Betteredge and Franklin hurried down to the shore and searched along the tideline. They soon found a girl's footprints leading out towards the rocks above the Shivering Sand.
Before evening a fisherman brought the sad news that Rosanna Spearman was dead. She had drowned in the Shivering Sand, and nobody could say how it had happened.
Betteredge grieved for Rosanna more than he had expected, and he asked himself whether he could have done more. For once, even Robinson Crusoe had no wise word to offer him.
Rachel declared that she could no longer stay in the house, so her mother took her to London. They left the next morning in a closed carriage, and Rachel did not once look back.
A few days later Lucy Yolland came limping up to the house, her eyes red with crying. She would speak to nobody but Mr Franklin Blake, and she looked at Betteredge as if she hated him.
Franklin met Lucy on the shore, and she told him bitterly that Rosanna had loved him. He had never noticed it, she said, and that had been the cruellest part.
Then Lucy gave him a letter from Rosanna, and she limped away along the beach without another word. Franklin read it at once, and it told him exactly where something lay hidden in the sand.
They went at once to the rock that the letter described, and they found a chain buried in the sand. When they pulled it, a small tin box came slowly up out of the shining sand.
Franklin opened the box, and inside it lay a white nightgown with a stain of yellow paint. On the cloth, in small neat letters, was sewn the name Franklin Blake.
Franklin said that he did not understand it and that he must go to London at once. Betteredge watched him leave, and here his own part of the story comes to an end.
The next part of the story was told by Miss Clack, a cousin of Rachel's who lived in London. She wrote it in a small, tidy hand, and she wrote it with great seriousness.
Miss Clack gave a religious leaflet to everyone she met, whether they wanted one or not. She slipped them under doors, into pockets and between the pages of other people's newspapers.
Lady Verinder had taken a house in Montagu Square, and Rachel had grown very quiet and thin there. Miss Clack called nearly every day, always with a new leaflet in her bag.
Miss Clack greatly admired her cousin Godfrey Ablewhite, who was famous as a speaker at meetings for good causes. She thought him the finest Christian gentleman in England, and she told everybody so.
Godfrey called at Montagu Square again and again, and he was gentle and helpful to everyone in the house. Lady Verinder, who liked him, began to look forward to his visits.
Then came the news that Rachel had agreed to marry Godfrey Ablewhite. Miss Clack was delighted, but others who knew Rachel's heart were not so sure.
Lady Verinder was worried by the engagement, but she could not move her daughter from her choice. Rachel only said that she was tired and wanted to be settled.
Mr Bruff, the family lawyer, was a dry, sharp man who did not like speeches. He said little about Godfrey, but he watched him closely whenever they met.
Franklin Blake had come back to London after months abroad, and he heard that Rachel was engaged. He went at once to Montagu Square, with a face that frightened the butler.
Franklin demanded to see Rachel at once, saying that he must know why she had turned against him. Lady Verinder, who had always liked him, did not have the heart to send him away.
After a long wait, Rachel came down and stood stiffly by the door. Franklin asked her, as gently as he could, what he had done to deserve her anger.
Rachel answered in a low, steady voice that she had seen him take the diamond with her own eyes. She had been standing at her bedroom door that night, and she had watched everything.
Franklin said he remembered nothing of it, and that he would never steal from her. Rachel did not believe him, and she told him bitterly not to lie.
Rachel said that she had kept her secret because she had loved him, and that this was the only reason she had told no one. She was ashamed of having loved such a man.
Franklin told her about the stained nightgown with his name in it, but it only seemed to prove her point. She turned her face away, and he went out of the house in despair.
Soon afterwards, Lady Verinder fell ill with a heart complaint, and the doctors shook their heads. Rachel hardly left her mother's bedside by day or by night.
Lady Verinder died quietly in the early summer, with her daughter beside her. Rachel was heartbroken, for her mother had been the one person who had always believed in her.
Mr Bruff read the will to the family, and it surprised some of them. Lady Verinder had put Rachel's money in a trust, so that Rachel could spend only the income.
When Godfrey understood that he would never touch Rachel's money, his smile became very stiff. His charm slipped for a moment, and Mr Bruff saw the face underneath it.
Within a few days Godfrey wrote to Rachel that the engagement must end. He said that they had been mistaken in each other, and Rachel was left alone in the world.
A year passed, and Franklin Blake took up the pen to tell his own part of the story. He was still haunted by Rachel's words, and he still hoped to clear his name.
Franklin returned to Yorkshire, because the only place that held answers was the house where it had happened. Old Betteredge met him at the gate, and he wept a little with joy.
Over tea in the kitchen, Betteredge gave Franklin all the news of the neighbourhood. Superintendent Seegrave had retired, Sergeant Cuff had gone, and poor Dr Candy had been very ill.
Franklin called on Dr Candy at his small house in the village, hoping that the doctor might remember something about the dinner. He was shown into the waiting-room by a stranger.

Ezra Jennings, the doctor's assistant, was a thin, dark man whose hair grew in patches of black and snowy white. His face was worn and gentle, and his eyes were the saddest that Franklin had ever seen.
Betteredge told him later that nobody in the village liked Ezra Jennings, because nobody knew where he had come from. People said that he had a dark past, but nobody could say what it was.
Ezra told Franklin in a quiet voice that he was a sick man, who had suffered terrible pain for many years. Every day he needed strong medicine to be able to work.
The two men walked across the hills together, and Franklin told Ezra the whole strange story of the diamond. He did not leave out Rachel's accusation, or the stained nightgown.
At last Ezra said that, during the doctor's fever, he had written down everything the sick man said. Some of the words had been about a diamond and about Mr Franklin Blake.
Franklin read the broken sentences by the light of the window. They were a muddle of half-words and gaps, but he felt that the muddle was trying to say something.
Ezra took the notes home and spent the whole night filling in the gaps between the words. By morning he believed that he knew exactly what the doctor had been trying to say.
Ezra explained that Dr Candy, to prove his promise, had secretly put laudanum in Franklin's brandy and water that night. The doctor had meant it as a joke, and as a cure for sleeplessness.
Franklin remembered the glass of brandy and water that he had carried up the stairs, and he had to sit down. He had drunk it all, and he had slept more heavily than he had slept for years.
Ezra explained that laudanum can have strange effects on a man whose nerves are already tired. Such a man may rise and act like a person who is awake, and remember nothing afterwards.
Slowly, with a growing sense of horror, Franklin understood what all of it meant. If he had been drugged, he might himself have taken the diamond in his sleep, without ever knowing it.
Franklin remembered how worried he had been about the Indians and the diamond that evening. In his dream, he said, he might have taken it only to keep it safe from them.
Ezra suggested that they should repeat that night exactly, with the same dose, the same room and the same conditions. Then they would see whether Franklin did the same thing again.
Franklin knew that the experiment would prove nothing unless some respected person watched it. He wrote at once to Mr Bruff, the lawyer, and asked him to come to Yorkshire.
Mr Bruff came to Yorkshire and listened to Ezra's reasons with a very sceptical face. In the end, however, he agreed that the experiment was worth trying, and he promised to watch.
Franklin wrote to Rachel and told her everything, and he begged her to come to Yorkshire and see the experiment with her own eyes. He did not know whether she would even read it.
In London, Rachel opened the letter by the window with trembling fingers. She read it three times, and the colour came slowly back to her pale face.
Rachel wrote back that very evening, in a few short lines, that she would come to Yorkshire. She would watch in secret, so that Franklin would not know that she was there.

The old sitting-room was put back exactly as it had been on the birthday night, with a false yellow stone in the drawer. Betteredge moved the furniture himself, and he remembered the place of every chair.
To make everything the same, Franklin gave up smoking again, and for days he slept very badly. He was a miserable companion, but he did it without complaint.
