On the evening of the experiment, Rachel arrived in a closed carriage at dusk. Mr Bruff met her quietly, and he took her to a hiding-place where she could see without being seen.
At the usual hour, Ezra measured out the dose carefully, exactly as Dr Candy had done a year before. Franklin drank the glass, and he went up to his bed.
Ezra and Mr Bruff sat in the dark passage outside Franklin's door and waited. The hours passed very slowly, and the only sound was the old clock in the hall.
Late in the night, the door opened slowly, and Franklin stood there in his nightclothes. His eyes were open, but they looked at nothing, and he did not seem to see the two men.
Franklin walked slowly down the passage and along the dark landing, and the two watchers followed him on tiptoe. He went by the way he had gone a year before, without a single mistake.
Franklin entered the sitting-room, opened the drawer of the cabinet and lifted out the false diamond. Rachel, who watched from the shadows, put her hand over her mouth and began to cry.
Franklin carried the false diamond back along the passage to his own room, and he laid it down there. Then he lay on his bed, and he fell at once into a deep sleep.
Mr Bruff shook Ezra's hand in the grey light of the passage and admitted that he had been wrong to doubt. The experiment had proved that Franklin could act in his sleep and know nothing of it.
Rachel stepped out of her hiding-place into the grey light, and her face was wet with tears. She understood at last that Franklin had never meant to steal her diamond.
Franklin woke at sunrise with a heavy head, and he saw Rachel standing beside his bed. For a moment he thought that he was still dreaming.
Rachel begged him to forgive her for doubting him, and he took her in his arms. There was nothing to forgive, he told her, because he had never stopped loving her.
Then they understood why Rosanna had hidden the stained nightgown, and why she had made another to put in its place. She had loved Franklin, and she had wished to save him.
When the joy had settled a little, Franklin said that the real diamond was still missing. If he had taken it to his room that night, then who had taken it away?
Mr Bruff said that whoever took the stone from Franklin's room must have known where it was. He thought it was time to call on an expert, and the man he had in mind was Sergeant Cuff.
Sergeant Cuff had retired to a cottage in Dorking, where he grew roses and read the newspapers. Mr Bruff wrote to him at once and begged him to come and listen.
Cuff arrived the next day with a rose in his coat and a look of quiet interest. He listened to the whole story of the experiment without a word, and he was clearly pleased.
Cuff began by asking who else had been in the house on the night of the birthday. He wanted to know who might have seen Franklin walking in his sleep.
Mr Bruff remembered the strange look on Godfrey's face when the will was read. Cuff asked quietly whether anybody knew if Godfrey had troubles with his money.
Cuff set his helpers to ask careful questions across London, and within a week he had news. Godfrey Ablewhite kept a second house in Northwood, and he had told no one about it.
Cuff also learned that Godfrey had spent a large sum of money held in trust for another person. It had to be paid back by a certain day, and Godfrey had no way to do it.

Cuff explained his theory to the others with the quiet patience of a man laying out a puzzle. Godfrey, who had stayed in the house, had seen Franklin carry the stone, and had taken it for himself from Franklin's room.
A stone like that was too famous to sell, Cuff said, so Godfrey would have borrowed money against it. His man, Cuff guessed, was Mr Luker, a moneylender who lived in Lambeth.
Cuff sent a quick-eyed boy called Gooseberry to watch Mr Luker's house day and night. He came back after a few days with something that surprised the detective.
Gooseberry also reported that Mr Luker had gone to his bank in Lombard Street with a small packet under his arm. Cuff guessed that the diamond was safely locked away there.
On the day when the loan was due, Cuff and his helpers waited near the bank in Lombard Street. They watched every man who went in, and they did not take their eyes from the door.
At noon, Godfrey Ablewhite arrived in a cab, looking pale and anxious. He paid his debt to Mr Luker, and he took a small packet from the bank.
Godfrey came out of the bank in a great hurry, and he kept looking behind him as he walked. Gooseberry slipped after him through the crowd, as quiet as a shadow.
At last Godfrey reached Tolliver's, a quiet old inn, and he signed the book with a false name. He wished to leave England quickly, and he hoped that nobody would find him there.
Late that night, the three Indians, who had followed Godfrey across London, slipped silently into his room. They had waited a year and more, and they were in no hurry.
In the morning, Godfrey was found dead in his bed, and the small packet had gone from his coat. The Indians had taken the diamond, and no one had seen them leave.
Cuff and Mr Bruff were called to the inn, and they stood beside the bed in grave silence. Though the name in the book was false, they knew the dead man at once as Godfrey Ablewhite.
The three Indians left England by the next ship, and Cuff explained that they had done only what their oath demanded. They had gone back to the temple, he said, to put right the old wrong.
In the spring, Franklin and Rachel were married in the village church, with old Betteredge in the front row. He wept, and he blew his nose, and he said that it was only the incense.
Some time later, a letter arrived from Mr Murthwaite in India. He had seen three men, shaved and in simple robes, at a great festival, and he had known them at once.
The three men carried the stone in a quiet procession to the holy city of Somnauth, said Mr Murthwaite. The crowd bowed as it passed, and no one dared to touch it.
Once more the great yellow diamond shone in the forehead of the moon god, exactly where it had shone for centuries. Nobody in England would ever see it again, and perhaps that was best.
C1C2: Centuries ago, a great yellow diamond blazed in the forehead of a Hindu statue of the moon god, and a legend said that its light rose and fell with the moon. Pilgrims travelled for weeks to stand in the glow of the stone, and they went home certain that they had looked into the eye of heaven itself. Nobody who saw it in the temple ever forgot the sight, and the memory of that yellow fire stayed with them for the rest of their lives.

Three Brahmin priests, charged by their faith with the protection of the jewel, were bound by a solemn oath to watch over it through every generation. As each guardian grew old, he handed his duty to a son, so that the vigil passed down the years like a family name. The oath was simple and terrible, for it allowed no rest while the stone was in danger.

According to an old legend, a terrible fate would fall on any man who seized the diamond by violence, and the misfortune would follow his family from one generation to the next. The priests believed the warning without a shadow of doubt, and they repeated it to every stranger who came near the shrine. Whether it was truth or only a story, it would be tested sooner than anyone expected.

Over the following centuries, war and conquest carried the stone from one hand to another, and its guardians followed it patiently wherever it went. By the year 1799 it lay among the treasures of the fortress of Seringapatam, where Tipu Sultan ruled, and where three watchful strangers had taken lodgings nearby. Their vow had made them wanderers and strangers in many lands, but it had never made them hopeless or weary of their task.

In May 1799 the English army stormed Seringapatam, and after a fierce struggle on the broken walls, its soldiers poured into the fortress like a tide. By evening the great stronghold had fallen, and its streets were filled with smoke, shouting and confusion. In such an hour, a man with no conscience might do whatever he pleased.

Among the English officers who entered the fortress was a young man named John Herncastle, who had heard tales of the famous yellow diamond and who dreamed of owning it. While his comrades fought in the streets, he slipped away alone and made his way through the dim passages of the palace. He seemed to know exactly where he was going, as though he had studied the plan of the palace for many weeks beforehand.

Herncastle found the room where the stone was kept, and by the end of that terrible night the diamond was his. Some men lay dead, and although his cousin saw him afterwards with the jewel in his hands, no one could swear exactly how it had been won. The priests had lost their treasure, and the Colonel, as he would later be called, had gained a secret.

Herncastle carried his prize back to England, and long before he arrived, rumours of the night at Seringapatam had travelled ahead of him. Old friends turned their backs when he entered a room, and his own sister, Lady Verinder, refused to speak to him ever again. He answered their scorn with a hard silence, and he never explained himself to anyone.

For nearly fifty years the Colonel lived alone in London behind locked doors, a lonely man who seldom went out and welcomed nobody. The few who knew him said that he lived in constant fear of three dark figures who seemed to haunt the pavements outside his house. Whatever peace his money might have bought him, he never found it, and his rich house grew colder with every passing year.

When the Colonel died in 1848, unmourned and alone, his will left the famous diamond to his niece, Rachel Verinder, to be hers on her eighteenth birthday. Lady Verinder, who had never forgiven her brother, suspected that this strange gift was his last act of revenge. Yet no one could say what harm a jewel might do to a happy girl, and so the plan went ahead, with Franklin Blake chosen to carry the stone north.

Gabriel Betteredge, who served Lady Verinder's household for most of his long life, has been asked to set down everything he remembers about the loss of the diamond. He lights his pipe, spreads out his papers and resolves to tell the plain truth in the order that it happened. He admits at once that he is no writer, but he knows the story better than anyone alive.

Betteredge trusts only one book in the world, and it is the story of Robinson Crusoe, which he has read more times than he can count. Whenever trouble threatens, he opens the old volume at random, and he swears that he always finds exactly the advice that he needs. His friends laugh at the habit, but he has never found a better counsellor.

Lady Verinder's great house stands in Yorkshire, within sound of the sea, with green fields on one side and a wild line of sandy hills on the other. Betteredge has lived and worked there for close to fifty years, and he knows every stair, every cupboard and almost every secret it contains. To him it is less a building than a small kingdom, and he thinks of himself as its faithful minister.

Lady Verinder is a widow of calm good sense, and she has managed her house and her fortune with a gentle and steady hand since her husband's death. She is generous to everyone who serves her, and she dislikes quarrels more than any other kind of trouble. Betteredge would have walked through fire for her without a moment's thought, and he would have been glad of the chance to do so.

Rachel is the only daughter of the house, a girl who will turn eighteen in June, proud and quick-witted and always sure of her own mind. She is generous to the servants, loyal to her friends and scornful of anything that smells of lies or cowardice. Betteredge adores her, and he is not at all ashamed to say so to anyone who cares to listen, or even to those who do not.

Betteredge's daughter Penelope serves as Rachel's maid, a quick, cheerful girl with sharp eyes and an even sharper tongue. Every evening she brings her father the news of the whole household, including every whisper from the drawing-room, whether he wishes to hear it or not. Without her chatter, Betteredge would have understood far less of what was happening beneath his own roof.

One of the housemaids, Rosanna Spearman, had once been a thief and had spent some time in a reformatory for her crimes. Lady Verinder, who believed that every sinner deserves a second chance, had taken her into the house to begin a better life. Only the lady and Betteredge knew the girl's history, and they had agreed to keep it quiet.

Rosanna was a thin, plain girl with one shoulder higher than the other, and she worked hard and spoke very little to anyone. The other maids thought her proud and secretive, and they could never understand why she preferred her own company to theirs. Betteredge, who saw more than he said, felt a growing pity for her, though he was far too shy to tell her so.

Not far from the house, between two rocky points on the shore, lay a deadly quicksand that the local people called the Shivering Sand. When the tide turned, its smooth brown surface began to tremble as though something were breathing beneath it, and anything that fell upon it was drawn down for ever. Even the bravest fisherman kept well away from it, and mothers in the nearby village warned their children never to go near the place.

In her free hours Rosanna Spearman often walked to the Shivering Sand and sat for a long time on a rock above it, staring down at the trembling surface. Betteredge scolded her kindly for the habit, but she answered that the dreadful place seemed to call to her, and she could not explain why. He went home that day with a heaviness in his heart that he could not shake.

One morning a letter arrived at the house announcing that Franklin Blake, the lady's nephew, was coming to stay for some weeks. Betteredge remembered him as a clever and lively boy who had once spent happy summers there, and the news filled him with delight. He did not yet know that the visitor would bring the diamond with him.

Franklin had spent most of his life abroad, studying in France, Germany and Italy, and Betteredge declared that he seemed to carry half a dozen different characters inside one skin. He could be gay, thoughtful or dreamy according to which country he had last been thinking of. Beneath all these disguises, the old man believed, there still lived the warm-hearted boy he remembered.

Before long the household learned that Franklin would carry the Colonel's diamond north, to be given to Rachel on her birthday. Lady Verinder, who still distrusted every gift from her brother, was visibly uneasy, but Rachel was as thrilled as any girl would be on hearing of a jewel. Betteredge noticed the difference between mother and daughter and wished, privately, that he could take the mother's side.

One hot afternoon Penelope came running to find her father, with the news that three Indian men in white clothes were standing at the front door. They had a small English boy with them, and their leader said, with an elaborate bow, that they were travelling jugglers who hoped to entertain the family. Betteredge went out at once, prepared to send them away, since he disliked strangers who arrived uninvited at a gentleman's door.

Before Betteredge could stop them, the men began to toss a set of bright brass balls into the air, catching them behind their backs with astonishing ease. The servants crowded at the windows and clapped, and Penelope stood laughing in the doorway while the afternoon sun flashed on the spinning brass. It was a charming performance, and it ended with a question that was not charming at all.

When the performance was over, the leader poured a little ink into the palm of the English boy and told him to stare into it. Then, in careful English, he asked whether a certain gentleman, newly arrived from foreign parts, was expected at the house that day. Betteredge felt a chill, for there was only one such gentleman, and he was Franklin Blake.

Betteredge ordered the men off the grounds at once and warned them that he would call the police if they ever came back. They bowed with perfect politeness and walked away down the drive, but he could not forget their calm faces, nor the question about the gentleman from foreign parts. He felt uneasy for the rest of the afternoon, though he could not have said why.

Franklin Blake arrived the next day in a hired carriage, cheerful and dusty and a little weary from his long journey, and he shook the old servant warmly by the hand. Betteredge, who had not seen him for many years, was so glad that he almost forgot to be formal. For a moment, the shadow of the Indian jugglers faded from his mind altogether.

Franklin explained that he had left the diamond in a bank in the nearby town of Frizinghall, because he thought it would be safer there than in a country house. He admitted, with a nervous laugh, that he had noticed some foreign gentlemen shadowing him all the way from London, and he could not decide whether to be amused or alarmed. Betteredge, remembering the jugglers, felt a cold prickle on the back of his neck.

That evening Betteredge told Franklin about the jugglers and the strange question they had asked beside the boy with the ink. For the first time since his arrival, the young man grew quiet and serious, and he sat for a long while without speaking. At last he said that the three men were almost certainly the priests of the old story, and that they would not give up easily.

In the days that followed, Franklin and Rachel grew rapidly into friends, and the old house echoed with their laughter and their teasing. Betteredge, who observed them with the sharp eyes of an old servant, began to suspect that the friendship might soon turn into something warmer. It was a pleasant suspicion, and he kept it carefully to himself, because he knew how quickly such things are noticed in a house.

Franklin was fond of painting, and he decided to surprise Rachel by decorating the door of her little sitting-room with a pattern of flowers and leaves. He enlisted Penelope as his assistant, and the girl, delighted at being trusted with a secret, agreed without a moment's hesitation. The plan seemed innocent enough at the time, and it was entered into with the lightest hearts in the whole county.

Franklin and Penelope worked on the door for the whole of that long afternoon, and Franklin mixed his own colours with the care of a true artist. By evening the pattern was finished and lovely, although one small corner of the paint had stubbornly refused to dry. Nobody gave it a second thought that evening, and the door was simply left alone to dry in the quiet of the sitting-room.

Rachel's sitting-room contained a small cabinet of Indian workmanship, painted in vivid colours and fitted with a number of narrow drawers. It was her favourite possession, and she kept her most treasured belongings inside it, including the letters she preferred nobody to read. Little did anyone suspect that it would soon hold the most dangerous object in England.

On the day before the birthday, Rachel's cousin Godfrey Ablewhite arrived from Frizinghall with his mother and his sisters, all in the best of spirits. He was a tall, fair, handsome gentleman with a warm smile, and he was famous for speaking at meetings in aid of every good cause in the country. Betteredge noticed that everyone he met seemed to love him on sight, and he wondered, a little uneasily, how that was possible.

On the morning of the birthday, Franklin and Godfrey rode together into Frizinghall to fetch the diamond from the bank where it had been kept. Betteredge watched them leave from the gate, and he searched the road and the hedges for any sign of white robes, but to his relief he saw nobody at all. He did not know that someone was already watching the house from the shadow of the trees and the far side of the hill.

Towards noon the two riders returned, and Franklin carried a small sealed package carefully inside his coat. The whole family gathered in the drawing-room to see it opened, and even Betteredge, who had no business there, found an excuse to linger near the door. A hush fell over the room as the wrapping was removed, and even the servants by the door leaned forward to see.

The Moonstone was as large as a plover's egg, and it glowed with a deep yellow light, like a drop of sunshine that had been caught and held captive. Rachel gasped with wonder as Franklin placed it in her hands, and for a long moment no one in the room made any sound at all. Even Betteredge, who distrusted jewels, had to admit that he had never seen anything so lovely.

Rachel pinned the great stone to the front of her white dress and turned this way and that before the looking glass, quite lost in delight. Her mother smiled bravely, but Betteredge could see that Lady Verinder was thinking of her dead brother, and of the shadow that his gift might bring. Franklin, meanwhile, could not take his eyes from Rachel's happy face, and he forgot for a moment that he was tired and anxious.

That evening, as the guests arrived for the birthday dinner, Rachel came slowly down the great staircase with the diamond glowing on the breast of her white dress. Every head in the hall turned towards her, and a murmur of admiration rose from the visitors like the sound of the sea. It was her proudest moment, and it would also be her last happy one for a very long time.

Some twenty guests sat down to the birthday dinner, and the long table glittered with silver, glass and the soft light of a hundred candles. Betteredge moved quietly behind the chairs, directing the footmen with small movements of his eyebrows and keeping a careful watch over every plate. Nothing, he told himself firmly, would go wrong at this table, so long as he kept his eyes open and his footmen sober.

Rachel sat near the middle of the table, and the diamond blazed on the breast of her white dress each time she turned her head. The guests tried to talk of the weather and the harvest, but their eyes kept returning to the stone like iron to a magnet. Rachel pretended not to notice, although she was plainly delighted by the attention and by the admiration of her cousins.

Between the soup and the fish, a lady leaned across the table and asked how the late Colonel had come to own such a stone. A silence followed, because the family knew the whispers about Seringapatam and were too polite to repeat them, and nobody could give her a clear answer. Lady Verinder looked down at her plate, and Betteredge saw that she had not eaten a single mouthful for some minutes.

Near the end of the table sat Mr Murthwaite, a tall, sunburnt and silent man who had travelled for years in the wildest parts of India, where few Englishmen had ever dared to go. He had barely spoken all evening, but his dark eyes had been resting on the diamond for some time. Betteredge, who could read a guest as easily as a clock, felt that something was about to be said.

When Rachel held out the stone, Mr Murthwaite studied it for a long time without a word, turning it slowly in the candlelight. At last he said, in a low voice, that its story was known from one end of India to the other, and that men had given their whole lives to follow it. The guests put down their forks to listen, and for a moment the only sound was the quiet hiss of the candles.

He told the guests that the Brahmins who had guarded the stone had never abandoned their search, and that their oath was passed from father to son like a house or a name. Fifty years, he said, were nothing to men who believed that they served their god, and they would wait another fifty if they had to. Somebody at the table laughed nervously and then stopped, as though the sound had seemed out of place in the warm, bright room.

Franklin leaned forward and described how three Indians had followed him through London, and how three men who looked very much like them had appeared at the door of the house that same week. Mr Murthwaite listened gravely, and he did not smile, which troubled Betteredge more than any speech could have done. The jugglers, he said, were not what they seemed, and he advised Franklin to take the matter far more seriously than he had so far.

Mr Murthwaite said that these men were Brahmins of high rank, who had surely given up their place among their own people by crossing the sea in pursuit of the stone. Such men, he warned, would not be bought, frightened or argued with, and they would not stop until the diamond was theirs again. He spoke without heat, and that made the warning all the worse, for a man who shouts is usually a man who can be ignored.

Lady Verinder looked anxiously at her daughter, and for a moment the whole room seemed to hold its breath. Then Godfrey Ablewhite, with the easy charm of a man used to quieting a crowded hall, made a good-humoured joke about jugglers and diamonds, and the company laughed with great relief. Only Betteredge noticed that Mr Murthwaite had not laughed at all, and that his dark eyes were still resting on the diamond.

When the laughter had faded, little Dr Candy, the doctor of the village and a man who could never resist a joke, noticed that Franklin looked pale and tired. He began to tease him about it in front of the whole table, with the cheerful cruelty of a man who thinks that every illness is a kind of comedy. Franklin only smiled and shrugged, and he said that he would sooner trust his own pillow than any doctor in the country.

Franklin admitted that he had slept very badly ever since he gave up his cigars, and that he lay awake for half of every night. Dr Candy declared with great confidence that this was a plain case of tired nerves, which any sensible doctor could mend in a week. Franklin, who had heard such promises before, only smiled politely and said that he would believe it when he saw it, or rather, when he slept it.

Franklin laughed and said that no doctor in England had ever cured a bad night's sleep, and that he doubted whether Dr Candy would be the first. The little doctor, rather offended, answered that he would make Mr Franklin sleep like a child, and that this was a promise. The argument ended in laughter, but Betteredge saw that the doctor's feelings had been bruised.

When the last of the dessert had been cleared away, the guests said their goodbyes and went out to their waiting carriages, one by one. Mr Murthwaite shook hands gravely with Lady Verinder and drove off through the moonlit lanes, still thinking, Betteredge supposed, of three men in white robes. By eleven o'clock the great house had grown quiet again, and only a few lights still burned in the upper windows.

Lady Verinder came to her daughter at the foot of the stairs and begged her, quite gently, to put the diamond somewhere safe for the night. She did not like having such a stone in the house at all, and she made no secret of her dislike. Rachel only kissed her and promised that nothing could possibly happen, and the mother, though unconvinced, said no more that night.

Rachel laid the diamond in one of the cabinet's narrow drawers, turned the key with a flourish, and slipped it on to her chain. Then she kissed her mother, said good night to Penelope, and went up to her bedroom with a face that was glowing like the stone itself. Betteredge heard the bedroom door close at last, and he felt a little easier for knowing that she was safe behind it.

As he did every night, Betteredge made his round of the house with the footman Samuel, testing every door and window to be sure that it was bolted. Tonight he took a good deal more care than usual, for the stories he had heard at dinner had left him thoroughly uneasy. The old house creaked in the dark as if it, too, were listening, and the shadows seemed to lean in towards the lamp.

When Betteredge unbolted the door to the terrace, he saw three figures standing perfectly still on the grass, their long pale robes silver in the moonlight. They were not hiding and they were not hurrying, but they were looking steadily at the windows of the house, as if counting them. Betteredge's heart gave one hard knock against his ribs, and he felt his hand tighten on the cold iron of the door-handle.

Betteredge gave a shout and ran across the grass with Samuel panting behind him, but the three men turned and walked away into the shadows, quite unhurried, as if they had all night. By the time the two servants reached the gate, the road lay empty and white in the moonlight, and there was not a footprint to be seen. It was most unsettling, and Betteredge, who had never been troubled by ghosts, found himself longing for the safety of the lamp.

Franklin, yawning widely, carried a glass of brandy and water up the stairs to his bedroom and wished the household good night. Betteredge thought nothing of it, for a tired man may well take a drink before bed, and he had troubles enough of his own to think about. He was wrong, as he would learn much later, to take so little notice.

One by one the lights went out, until the great house stood dark and silent under the moon, with its doors locked and its secrets asleep inside. The wind had dropped, the sea lay still beyond the sand, and nobody in the house heard so much as a footstep. It was, Betteredge thought afterwards, the quietest night he had ever known, and it was the last quiet night for a very long while.

Next morning, Betteredge woke early, and in the cheerful light of day the three white shapes on the terrace seemed far less alarming than they had in the dark. He was settling down to his breakfast with a quiet mind when he heard the sound of someone running along the passage. In all his fifty years, he had never liked the sound of running in a quiet house.

Penelope burst through the door, pale and out of breath, and cried that the diamond had vanished from Miss Rachel's cabinet. Betteredge told her sharply not to talk nonsense, but the girl only clung to the table and shook her head, and he saw that she was telling the truth. He had left his breakfast untouched before he knew it, and he was already halfway to the door of the passage.

The Indian cabinet stood in its corner exactly as it had stood the night before, with its painted birds and flowers shining in the sunlight, but the small drawer hung open and there was nothing in it. Betteredge looked inside twice, and then felt along the bottom with his fingers, as if a diamond the size of a plover's egg could be hiding there. The silence in the room was dreadful, and it seemed to press upon his ears like deep water.

Rachel stood in the doorway of her bedroom, white as paper and strangely calm, with her eyes fixed on the empty drawer. When Betteredge spoke to her, she did not seem to hear him, and when he spoke again, she turned away and closed her door without a sound. He had expected tears, or anger, but he had not expected silence, and the silence frightened him far more than either.

Penelope fetched Lady Verinder, who came quickly in her morning dress and stared at the empty drawer without a word. A woman of lesser sense might have wept or fainted, but Lady Verinder only drew a long breath and asked quietly where her daughter was. She knocked gently on Rachel's door, and it did not open, and she stood a long moment with her hand against the wood.

Franklin arrived a moment later with a coat thrown over his shoulders, still heavy-eyed with sleep, and he could hardly believe what he saw. He said again and again that the stone had been safe in the bank for a month, and that he had carried it across the whole county without losing it. He looked, Betteredge thought, quite ill, and he sat down heavily on the edge of a chair as if his legs had failed him.

Before breakfast was over, the news had run through the house from the cellars to the attics and out to the stables beyond. The servants whispered in corners, the maids huddled together in the passage, and the word Indians was on every tongue. Betteredge sent them all back to work with a voice that he rarely used, but he knew that no work would be done that day.

Betteredge went around the whole house again with a sinking heart, and he found every bolt exactly where he had left it and every window whole. There were no footprints on the terrace, no marks on the sills, and the dew lay smooth and unbroken across the grass. If a thief had come, he had come like a ghost, and he had gone the same way.

Franklin said at once that the three Indians must have done it, since they had followed the stone across the world and had been seen on the terrace only hours before. Betteredge agreed that it looked likely, but he reminded him that no stranger could have entered a house which had been locked so carefully, and that nothing had been forced. The puzzle only grew deeper with every question they asked, and every answer seemed to lead them back to the same locked doors.

Lady Verinder decided that the police must be called without a moment's delay, and Betteredge, who agreed with her, gave the orders himself. A groom saddled the fastest horse in the stable and galloped away down the drive to Frizinghall, and Betteredge watched him out of sight with a heavy heart. He did not yet know how little the police could do, nor how many weeks would pass before the matter was properly begun.

Superintendent Seegrave arrived at eleven o'clock, a stout, solemn man in a uniform that seemed a little too tight for him, with a loud voice and a very good opinion of himself. He announced to the household that he had solved harder cases than this one, and that the thief would be in prison before the day was out. Betteredge hoped, without much faith, that he was right, for the sake of Lady Verinder and the peace of the house.

Seegrave went straight to the sitting-room and examined the cabinet, the window, the lock and the carpet with enormous seriousness, writing in his notebook after each one. He said “Hm” a good many times, and he looked so wise that Betteredge was nearly convinced, until he noticed that the man had trodden on the very place where footprints might have been. It was not a promising beginning, and Betteredge's heart sank a little further with every solemn word that the man uttered.

Seegrave then announced that every servant's room, and every servant's box, must be searched from top to bottom for the missing stone, beginning with the maids. The women were furious at being treated like thieves, and Penelope declared that she would leave the house that very hour if a policeman touched her things. It was Lady Verinder who finally restored some peace, by appearing in the hall and speaking quietly to her angry maids.

Betteredge told the superintendent, with some heat, that most of the servants had served the family faithfully for many years, and that to search their belongings would be an insult to honest people. Seegrave answered that the law was the law, and that an honest servant had nothing to fear. It was the kind of remark that makes an honest man angrier than any insult.

Seegrave soon noticed that one housemaid, Rosanna Spearman, looked pale and ill and stood a little apart from the others, as she always did. When he heard that she had once been in prison for theft, his eyes began to shine like those of a dog that has smelled a rabbit. Betteredge had to bite his tongue, because he knew that the girl had been given a second chance in this very house.

Seegrave knocked at Rachel's bedroom door and politely requested a few minutes of her time, but she refused to open it. Through the wood she sent word that she wished to see no policeman, and that she knew nothing whatever about the matter. Seegrave went away offended, and Lady Verinder, who had never seen her daughter behave like this, stood in the passage with a puzzled face.

Seegrave decided that the three Indian jugglers must be the thieves, since they had been seen near the house and had already asked questions about the diamond. He sent two constables galloping to Frizinghall with orders to arrest them as rogues and vagabonds, and by evening the three men were safely in the police cells. The superintendent was very pleased with himself, and he went about the house with the satisfied air of a man whose work is nearly done.

The next day the three Indians stood before the magistrate in Frizinghall, calm, courteous and as upright as three trees. They spoke excellent English, they answered every question patiently, and they showed not the slightest sign of fear or guilt, which Seegrave took as proof of cunning and everyone else took as proof of innocence. The leader merely asked what crime they were supposed to have committed, and nobody in the court could give him a plain answer.

The magistrate found that the men had been seen in Frizinghall at the hour of the theft, miles from the house, and that no stone was found on them or in their lodgings. He set them free with an apology, and Seegrave, who had boasted so loudly that morning, went red to the roots of his hair. Betteredge, for once, did not enjoy another man's embarrassment, since he knew that the real thief was still at large somewhere.

When Franklin heard the news, he said that the superintendent was hopeless and that a cleverer man must be found at once, whatever it cost. He remembered that his family lawyer, Mr Bruff, knew of a famous detective in London who had solved cases that had baffled every other officer in England. He went off to write a letter that same afternoon, and his pen scratched so hard that Betteredge could hear it in the passage.

Franklin wrote to Mr Bruff in London that very afternoon, describing the theft and begging him to send down Sergeant Cuff by the first train he could find. A groom carried the letter to the station at a gallop, and the household settled down to a long, uneasy wait. Betteredge, who found waiting harder than work, went out and counted the hens, and then counted them all over again.

While the house waited, Franklin noticed a long smear across the pretty pattern that he had painted on Rachel's door. The paint had still been wet when everyone went to bed, which meant that somebody had brushed against it during the night, and that this somebody might have carried a mark away on his clothes. Seegrave, strangely, had never noticed it, though he had spent a whole morning in the room with his notebook and his important frown.

Penelope remembered that the paint had still been wet when she said good night to Rachel, a little before midnight, and that nobody had touched it then. That meant the smear had been made some time between midnight and the discovery of the theft, and it was one of the few clues in the whole sad affair. Franklin looked at it for a long time, and he did not seem to hear Betteredge when he spoke to him.

The whole house had become uneasy, and each servant wondered privately about all the others, though nobody dared to say so aloud. Even old friends spoke to one another in low voices, the cook let her bread burn for the first time in thirty years, and the kitchen, which had always been the happiest room in the house, was cold and silent. Suspicion is a slow poison, and it was working quietly in the house, turning friend against friend and servant against servant.

Franklin knocked at Rachel's door several times and begged her to talk to him, but she would not come out, and when she did appear, she looked at him with cold, angry eyes. He had been her closest friend only a week before, and Betteredge could see that the change had cut him to the heart. He bore it silently, as a gentleman should, but Betteredge noticed that he ate almost nothing at breakfast or at dinner.

Sergeant Cuff arrived by the afternoon train, a lean, grey and melancholy man in a plain black coat who looked more like a gentleman's gardener than a famous detective. His eyes were a pale, steely grey, and they seemed to travel straight through whatever they rested upon, as though they could see the backs of people's thoughts. Betteredge felt a little afraid of him at once, and he found himself standing straighter and speaking more carefully than usual.

Before he looked at a single clue, Sergeant Cuff asked in his soft, sad voice to be shown the garden, for he had heard of the old roses at the house and wished to see them. Betteredge, who had expected a man of iron, found himself leading the world's most famous detective between the flower beds. It was the oddest start to an inquiry that he could remember, and he wondered whether the great man was laughing at them all.

Cuff and the old gardener, Mr Begbie, were soon deep in an argument about white moss roses and the proper way to grow them, and neither would give way. Cuff declared that nothing was better for a rose than soap and water, and Mr Begbie replied that nothing was worse, and the quarrel promised to last until midnight. Betteredge, in despair, reminded them both of the missing diamond, and begged them to leave the roses until the thief was caught.

At last Cuff followed Betteredge into the house and went straight to the sitting-room, where he thanked Superintendent Seegrave very politely for all his work and then, just as politely, asked him to leave the room. The superintendent went off in great offence, and he did not return, which Betteredge felt was no great loss to the investigation. Cuff stood alone in the quiet room for a minute, looking at the empty drawer, the open window and the stained door.

Cuff stood for a long moment in silence, and then he told Betteredge, in a voice that was almost kind, that the three Indians had not taken the diamond. Whoever had done this thing, he said, was somebody who slept under this roof, and he would find the person long before the roses had finished flowering. Betteredge felt the floor tilt a little under his feet, for he had never dreamed that the thief might be one of his own people.

Sergeant Cuff took a small glass from his waistcoat pocket and studied the smear on the door for a very long time, moving along it an inch at a time. Then he stepped back to the far side of the room and looked at it again, with his head on one side, as a painter might study his own picture. Betteredge held his breath and said nothing, for he felt that a single word might break the spell of the detective's attention.

At last Cuff announced that the mark had been made by a piece of cloth, and by the shape of it a nightgown, brushing against the door in the dark. Whoever had worn that garment, he explained, must have a stain of yellow paint on it somewhere, and that stain would be the best witness of all. He said it so quietly that Betteredge hardly noticed the weight of what he had said.

Cuff asked Lady Verinder for leave to examine the nightclothes of everybody who slept in the house, from the family down to the kitchen-maid. She was reluctant, for she hated the idea of treating her people like suspects, but she gave her permission because she wanted the truth more than she wanted comfort. Cuff thanked her with a small bow, and he promised that nothing would be disturbed more than was strictly necessary.

Cuff asked to see the washing-books, in which the laundry maid recorded every garment that went to the wash, and he read them page by page with the patience of a man doing a long sum. Every nightgown in the house, he found, was properly counted, and he checked each name against the list of owners until his eyes grew tired. Betteredge could not see where all this was leading, but he went on fetching books and lamps like an obedient child.

When the long task was done, Cuff announced that every nightgown in the house was accounted for, except one that had vanished from the wash since Thursday. Its owner, he said, had hidden or destroyed it, and whoever had done so had a reason for wanting nobody to see it. The silence in the room was heavy with all that this meant, and Betteredge found that he did not dare to ask a single question.

Penelope remembered that Rosanna had said she was ill on the Thursday, and that afterwards she had shut herself in her room with the door locked, as though she were sewing something she wished no one to see. The girl had also walked alone to Frizinghall that afternoon and returned with a parcel under her arm, and she had been quiet and strange ever since. Betteredge listened with a sinking heart, for he could not bear to think that Rosanna had anything to do with such trouble.

Cuff asked to see the famous Shivering Sand about which he had heard so much, so Betteredge led him down the cliff path to the shore. As they walked, the detective asked a good many quiet questions about Rosanna Spearman, and Betteredge, against his will, found himself answering every one of them. The sea wind blew cold across their faces, and the gulls wheeled and cried above the tide as though they too were curious.

Far off along the sand, Betteredge saw a thin figure on the rocks, and he knew without any doubt that it was Rosanna Spearman, standing where she so often stood. She saw the two men, drew back sharply like a creature that had been caught, and hurried away across the shingle with her head bent low. Cuff watched her go without a word, and then he took out his black notebook and wrote something down in very small letters.

Cuff said quietly that the girl was hiding something, and that, whatever it was, it had something to do with this lonely stretch of sand. He added that he was not yet sure whether she had stolen the diamond herself, or whether she was only shielding someone else who had. Betteredge, who had liked Rosanna, could not tell which possibility he feared more, and he walked on beside the detective in gloomy silence.

Betteredge told him that Rosanna's only friend in the world was Lucy Yolland, a lame, sharp-tongued fisherman's daughter who lived in a cottage near the shore and hated the whole world except Rosanna. Cuff said that he would like to talk to Lucy Yolland before the week was out, and he made a note of the name in a small black book. The detective, it seemed, forgot nothing, and Betteredge began to feel that he would never again tell a lie in the man's presence.

Cuff told Lady Verinder that he could go no further without speaking to Rachel herself, since the girl had been the last person to see the diamond. Her mother agreed to ask her, though she was far from sure that Rachel would consent. To everyone's surprise, a few minutes later the young lady came downstairs, as straight and silent as a figure in a painting.

Rachel entered the drawing-room with her head held high, as pale and straight as a candle, and she looked at Cuff as though he were something that had been left on the carpet. She answered his questions in the shortest words she could find, and sometimes she did not answer them at all. Betteredge had never seen her so cold, and he could not make out whether her eyes were angry or only frightened.

Cuff asked her gently when she had last seen the stone, and whether any other person in the world possessed a key to the cabinet. Rachel replied that she had locked the diamond away with her own hands and kept the key on her own chain, and she folded her lips as though she meant to say nothing further. Cuff bowed and thanked her, but his grey eyes were very busy, and they seemed to be counting every movement she made.

Rachel left the room as suddenly as she had entered it, and the door closed behind her with a very small and decided click. Cuff stood for a moment in silence, and then he said, half to himself, that the young lady knew a great deal more than she was willing to tell. Betteredge felt his temper begin to rise, and he clenched his fists behind his back so that nobody should see them.

In a low voice, Cuff told Betteredge his suspicion that Miss Rachel had hidden the diamond herself, in order to raise money for some secret purpose that she dared not admit to her mother. Young ladies, he explained, sometimes fall into debt for reasons that they are ashamed to tell, and a stone like that one could pay a great many bills. He had seen such cases before, he said, and in nearly every one the young lady had hidden the truth for the sake of her pride.

Betteredge answered in a rage that Cuff must be out of his mind to say such a thing of Miss Rachel, whom he had known since she was a baby in arms. She was the proudest, truest and most honest girl in England, he said, and she had never owed anyone a penny in her life. Cuff only sighed and said that he was sorry to have given pain, but that a detective must say what he truly thinks.

When Lady Verinder heard what Cuff thought, her face turned white with anger, and she rose from her chair as straight as a soldier. She said that no man living had the right to accuse her daughter of stealing her own diamond, and that she would hear no more of it in her house. Never before had Betteredge heard her speak so sharply, and he was quite proud of her, though he did not say so.

Lady Verinder thanked Cuff coldly for his trouble, paid his fee, and informed him that his help was no longer wanted in her house. He bowed with perfect politeness, put on his hat and walked out of the door without a trace of offence, as if he had been dismissed a hundred times before. At the gate he stopped and looked back with a sad smile, as a man might look at a house he does not expect to see again.

At the gate Cuff took Betteredge aside and told him to keep a careful eye on Rosanna Spearman, who, he said, would soon do something very strange indeed. He added that the diamond would turn up again in the end, as such things always did, and that his address was in London if the family should ever need him. Then he went down the road, thinking about roses, and Betteredge, watching his thin figure grow smaller, felt strangely deserted.

The next morning Rosanna Spearman did not come down to her work, and when Penelope went to look for her, the bed had not been slept in and the girl was nowhere in the house. She had put on her hat and her shawl and walked out without telling a soul, and nobody had seen her go. Betteredge remembered Cuff's words at the gate with a cold shiver, and he began at once to search every room of the great house.

Betteredge and Franklin hurried down to the shore and searched the whole length of the beach, calling her name into the wind. They soon found a line of small footprints crossing the wet sand towards the rocks above the Shivering Sand, and they followed it with growing dread. At the end of it lay only the quiet, shining sand, which gave no sign of what had passed there and no answer to their calls.

Before evening a fisherman came up to the house with his cap in his hand and brought the sad news that Rosanna Spearman was dead. She had drowned in the Shivering Sand, which gives up its victims reluctantly if at all, and nobody could say for certain how it had happened. Betteredge sat down heavily on the kitchen chair and said nothing for a long time.

Betteredge grieved for Rosanna more than he had ever expected to, and he asked himself again and again whether a kinder word from him might have changed her fate. He took down his old copy of Robinson Crusoe and opened it at random, but for once the book had no wise word to offer, and he closed it gently. The house felt twice as empty as before, and for days afterwards no one in the kitchen could bear to sing or even to whistle.

Rachel declared that she could no longer bear to stay in the house where so much had gone wrong, and Lady Verinder, who would have done anything for her, agreed to take her to London. They left the next morning in a closed carriage with the blinds half drawn, and Rachel did not once look back. Nor did she look at Franklin, who stood in the drive with his hat in his hand and watched the carriage until the dust hid it.

A few days later Lucy Yolland came limping up to the house, her eyes red with crying and her whole thin face fierce with grief, and demanded to see Mr Franklin Blake. She would not say a word to Betteredge, and she looked at him as though he and all his kind were responsible for her friend's death. Betteredge was too sorry for her to be angry, and he stood aside at the gate and let her pass without a word.

Franklin met Lucy on the shore, where the wind whipped her shawl about her, and she told him bitterly that poor Rosanna had loved him from the first day he came to the house. He had never once noticed it, she said, and that, perhaps, had been the cruellest part of all. Franklin stood very still, with a look of dawning pain, as though a door he had not known about had suddenly been opened.

Then Lucy took a thick folded letter from inside her dress and put it into his hand, saying that Rosanna had written it for him and for nobody else, and she limped away along the beach without another word. Franklin read it standing in the wind, with Betteredge looking anxiously over his shoulder, and in careful words it told him where Rosanna had hidden something in the sand. She begged him not to think too hardly of her, and she signed it with her name and nothing more.

They went at once to the rock that the letter described, and there, half buried in the sand, they found a thin chain which led into the depths. When Franklin pulled it, hand over hand, a small tin box rose slowly and reluctantly from the shining sand, dripping with water. Betteredge thought of the girl who had hidden it there, and who had come day after day to sit above the place.

Franklin opened the box with an unsteady hand, and inside it lay a white nightgown, stained across the front with a smear of yellow paint. On the cloth, in small and careful stitches, was sewn the plain name of Franklin Blake, and not even his own memory could explain it. For a long moment neither man could speak, and the only sound was the slow sigh of the sea over the sand.

Franklin said hoarsely that he did not understand it at all, and that he must go to London that very night to find Rachel and learn the truth. Betteredge watched him go, an old man alone at a gate, and with that parting his own part of the story comes to an end. Others, wiser or at least better informed, would tell what came after, and Betteredge was content to lay down his pen.

The next part of the story was told by Miss Clack, a poor cousin of Rachel's who lived alone in London and was extremely devout. She wrote it in a small, tidy hand, with many underlinings, because she believed that every sentence ought to improve the reader's soul. Her version of events would be very different from Betteredge's, for she saw everything through the spectacles of a pious and curious woman.

Miss Clack pressed a religious leaflet on everyone she met, whether they wanted one or not, and nobody ever managed to refuse. She slipped them under doors, into coat pockets and between the pages of other people's newspapers, and she believed that she had thereby saved a great many souls. Her relatives, who had saved nothing but their patience, bore it with gentle smiles.

Lady Verinder had taken a tall house in Montagu Square, where Rachel, who had grown thin and quiet since the summer, spent her days in the drawing-room with a book she did not read. Miss Clack called nearly every afternoon, always with a fresh leaflet in her bag, and she observed everything with the sharp eyes of a woman who had plenty of time. Little escaped her notice, and whatever she noticed she wrote down afterwards in her careful, underlined hand.

Miss Clack admired no one more than her cousin Godfrey Ablewhite, who was famous across London as a speaker at meetings for every good cause under the sun. She thought him the finest Christian gentleman in England, and she said so to anyone who would listen, and to several who would not. Godfrey, for his part, accepted her praise with a modest smile, as a man accepts a coin that he has fully earned.

Godfrey called at Montagu Square again and again, and he was so gentle, so cheerful and so thoughtful that he soon became the favourite of the whole house. Lady Verinder, who had been low in spirits, began to look forward to his visits, and even Rachel gave him her rare smile. Nobody asked what he was really hoping to gain, because it seemed unkind to ask such a question of so good a man.

Then came the surprising news that Rachel had accepted an offer of marriage from Godfrey Ablewhite, who had asked her after only a few weeks of visits. Miss Clack was delighted beyond words, but those who knew Rachel's heart best were less sure, and wondered why a girl who had loved so warmly should choose so coolly. Perhaps she wished to forget, and perhaps a quiet marriage to an agreeable man seemed to her the shortest road to peace.

Lady Verinder was uneasy about the engagement, though she could not have said exactly why, and she tried gently to persuade her daughter to wait. Rachel, however, would not be moved, and replied only that she was tired and wanted to be settled and at peace. A mother can argue with a child, but she can seldom argue with a broken heart, and Lady Verinder gave way at last.

Mr Bruff, the family lawyer, was a dry, sharp-eyed man who had never been taken in by a speech in his life, and he said very little about Godfrey. He watched him closely, however, whenever the two of them met in the same room, and he made a number of private notes that he did not share. Miss Clack found him cold and worldly, and she observed with some severity that a man who despised eloquence could scarcely be a man of deep feeling.

Franklin Blake had come back to London after months of restless travel abroad, and at his club he heard the news of Rachel's engagement from a stranger. He went at once to Montagu Square, and the look on his face was such that the old butler, who had admitted many callers, stepped back to let him pass. Miss Clack happened to be in the hall, with a bundle of leaflets under her arm and her ears wide open.

Franklin demanded to see Rachel at once, declaring that he could bear no more silence and that he must know why she had turned against him so cruelly. Lady Verinder, who had always liked him and could not bring herself to think him guilty, did not have the heart to send him away. She went upstairs to speak to her daughter herself, and the whole house waited in suspense for the sound of her step.

After a long wait, Rachel came slowly down to the drawing-room and stood stiffly by the door, as pale as a ghost, with her hand on the handle. Franklin asked her, as gently as he could, what he could possibly have done to deserve her anger and her silence. Miss Clack, who ought to have left the room, sat very still behind a screen.

Rachel answered in a low, steady voice that she had seen him take the diamond with her own eyes, for she had been awake at her bedroom door that night and had watched him cross the room. He had opened the drawer, she said, taken out the stone and walked away without a glance behind him. Franklin looked at her as though she had struck him, and the colour drained from his face until it was nearly white.

Franklin said hoarsely that he remembered nothing of the kind and that he would sooner have cut off his hand than steal from her. Rachel, who had been waiting for months for his confession, did not believe a word of it, and she told him bitterly not to add lies to his wrong. It was the cruellest moment of all, and even Miss Clack, hidden behind her screen, felt her heart grow heavy.

Rachel said, with her eyes bright with tears, that she had kept her secret from the police and from her own mother only because she had loved him, and that she was ashamed of that love now. Franklin looked from her face to her mother's, and he understood that both of them believed him a thief. The room seemed to spin around him, and he held on to the back of a chair to keep from falling.

Franklin told her about the stained nightgown that Rosanna had hidden, with his own name sewn inside it, but the story only seemed to prove her point, and she turned her face to the wall. He went out of the house in despair, still unable to remember anything at all about that dreadful night. Miss Clack, peeping out from behind the screen, felt that she had never witnessed such a scene in all her years of visiting.

Soon afterwards, Lady Verinder fell gravely ill with a heart complaint, and although the best doctors in London attended her, they shook their heads gloomily in the passage. Rachel, who had at last forgotten her own troubles, scarcely left her mother's bedside by day or by night. Miss Clack came every morning with comfort and a fresh leaflet, and she was not at all discouraged when the patient fell asleep over it.

Lady Verinder died quietly in the early summer, with her daughter at her side, and the whole house sank into a deep and heavy stillness. Rachel was heartbroken, for her mother had been the one person in the world who had always loved her without question, and she felt more alone than ever before. Even Miss Clack was silent for a day, which those who knew her declared to be the surest proof of the house's sorrow.

Mr Bruff read the will aloud to the little family circle, and it contained a surprise for some of them. Lady Verinder had placed Rachel's fortune in a trust, so that Rachel received only the income for her life, and neither she nor any husband could touch the money itself. Mr Bruff watched Godfrey's face as he read, and he did not like what he saw.

When Godfrey understood that he could never lay a finger on Rachel's money, his handsome smile became rather stiff, and his famous charm slipped for a moment like a mask. Mr Bruff caught a glimpse of the face underneath, and he put it away carefully in his memory. Within the hour Godfrey had remembered an urgent engagement elsewhere, and he left the house with a smile that no longer reached his eyes.

Within a few days Godfrey wrote a smooth, regretful letter to say that, after much prayer, he and Rachel had been mistaken in each other and must part as friends. Rachel read it without surprise and without a tear, and she was left alone in the world with her grief and her secret. Only Mr Bruff remained to guard her interests, and he took up the task with a dry and faithful determination.

A year passed, and Franklin Blake took up the pen to tell his own part of the story, for nobody else could describe what he felt. He was still haunted by Rachel's words in the drawing-room, and he still hoped, against all reason, to find some proof that would clear his name. His wanderings had brought him nothing but weariness, and the further he travelled, the nearer the old puzzle seemed to follow.

Franklin returned to Yorkshire, because the only place that could hold any answers was the house where it had all happened, and the only man who might help him was the old steward who had seen everything. Betteredge met him at the gate and wept a little with joy, though he pretended that it was only the wind. The great house stood empty and quiet, with its shutters closed and its garden growing wild around the terrace.

Over tea in the kitchen, Betteredge gave Franklin all the news of the neighbourhood, in no particular order. Superintendent Seegrave had been moved to another district, Sergeant Cuff had retired to grow roses somewhere in the south, and poor Dr Candy had nearly died of a fever which had left his memory a blank. Franklin listened with growing interest, and when the old man had finished, he asked to be taken at once to the doctor's house.

Franklin went to call on Dr Candy at his small house in the village, hoping that the little doctor might remember something from the night of the birthday dinner that would throw some light on the mystery. Instead he was shown into the waiting-room by a stranger, a tall and curiously striking man whom he had never seen before. The stranger introduced himself as Ezra Jennings, and he bowed with a grace that did not seem to belong to a mere assistant.

Ezra Jennings, the doctor's new assistant, was a tall, thin, sallow man whose hair grew in curious patches of black and snowy white, as if two heads had been shuffled together. His face was lined and gentle, his voice was low, and his eyes were the saddest and most intelligent that Franklin had ever met. Franklin felt drawn to him at once, though he could not have explained what it was that made him trust the stranger.

Betteredge told him later that nobody in the village could abide Ezra Jennings, simply because nobody knew where he had come from or what he had done before he arrived. People whispered darkly that there must be some secret in his past, though no one could say what it was. Franklin, who knew what it was to be suspected, found that he liked Ezra all the more for it.

Ezra told Franklin, in a quiet voice, that he was a sick man who had suffered cruel pain for many years, and that every day he needed a strong medicine simply to be able to work. He did not complain, and he spoke of it as another man might speak of the weather. Franklin could not help admiring his courage and patience, and he said so, which seemed to surprise the sick man very much.

The two men walked across the hills together that afternoon, and Franklin, who had not spoken of the matter to a stranger in a year, found himself telling Ezra the whole strange story of the diamond. He did not leave out Rachel's accusation or the stained nightgown, and Ezra listened without once interrupting. At the end he was quiet for a long time, and then he asked a question that made Franklin's heart beat faster.

At last Ezra said that during Dr Candy's fever, he had made a habit of writing down everything that the sick man muttered in his delirium, simply to pass the long nights. Some of the words, he added, had been about a diamond, and about a birthday dinner, and about Mr Franklin Blake. He asked whether Franklin would care to see them, since they might perhaps throw a little light upon the old mystery.

Franklin read the broken sentences by the last light of the window, and they seemed at first to be no more than a muddle of half-words, gaps and unfinished phrases. Yet a pattern was struggling to appear in the confusion, and he felt, with a strange prickling on his skin, that the confusion was trying to tell him something. Ezra watched his face carefully, as a doctor watches a patient who is about to hear something important.

Ezra took the notes home and spent the whole night arranging the broken sentences, filling in the gaps with the words that the doctor's sick mind must have meant. By morning he believed that he knew exactly what Dr Candy had been trying to say, and that it was far more important than either of them had guessed. He did not sleep at all, and when Franklin called in the morning, he was waiting at the door with a lamp still burning.

Ezra explained to him that Dr Candy, in order to keep his promise about the sleeplessness, had secretly put a dose of laudanum into Franklin's brandy and water on the night of the birthday. He had meant it as a cure and a harmless joke, Ezra said, and he had told no one, for he had been rather ashamed. Franklin's mouth fell open, and for a moment he could not find a single word to answer the quiet man in front of him.

Franklin remembered the glass of brandy and water that he had carried so innocently up the stairs, and he had to sit down in the nearest chair. He had drunk it to the last drop, and he had slept more deeply that night than he had slept for months, and in the morning he had thought only that the doctor's cure had worked. The truth was stranger than any dream, and it fitted every piece of the puzzle that had tormented him for a year.

Ezra explained that laudanum can have curious effects on a man whose nerves are already worn thin by sleeplessness, and who has lately given up a habit as strong as tobacco. Such a man, he said, may rise from his bed and act like one who is awake, with a purpose and a plan, and recall nothing at all the next morning. Franklin listened in amazement, and the more he heard, the more clearly he saw the whole dark night laid out before him.

Slowly, with a kind of horror that crept up his back like cold water, Franklin began to understand what all of it meant. If he had been drugged, then he might himself have taken the diamond from the cabinet while he slept, in just the way that Rachel had seen him do it, and without the least memory of it afterwards. The accusation which had broken his heart was true, and he was innocent at the same time.

Franklin remembered how deeply he had worried that evening about the Indians and their intentions, and how he had carried the responsibility for the stone since it left London. In his drugged sleep, he said slowly, he might well have taken the diamond from the cabinet merely to keep it safe from them. It was a theory that would fit the facts, and he longed to prove it.

Ezra suggested that they ought to repeat that night in every particular, with the same dose of the same drug, the same room, the same hour, and the same state of mind. If Franklin walked to the cabinet again, he said, then no one could doubt the truth, and Rachel would have to believe it too. It was a bold idea, and a little frightening, but it was also the only road that seemed to lead anywhere at all.

Franklin knew that the experiment would prove nothing unless some respectable and unbiased person watched it from beginning to end, and he knew exactly whom to ask. He wrote at once to Mr Bruff, the lawyer, setting out the whole story and begging him to come to Yorkshire as a witness. The answer came by return of post, and it was a cautious yes, written in the careful hand of a man who gives nothing away.

Mr Bruff came to Yorkshire by the first train and listened to Ezra's reasoning with the sceptical face of a man who had heard many wonderful theories. When Ezra finished, however, he was silent for a long minute, and then he agreed that the experiment was worth trying, and he promised to watch it himself. Franklin could have embraced him, but he contented himself with a handshake that nearly crushed the lawyer's fingers.

Franklin wrote a long letter to Rachel in which he told her everything that Ezra had discovered, and he begged her to come to Yorkshire and see the experiment for herself. He did not know whether she would even open it, for she had refused to read his letters for a year. He sealed it with a prayer and posted it, and then he began the longest wait that he had ever known.

In London, Rachel opened the letter by the window with trembling fingers, expecting more of the same bitter explanations that she had received before. She read it three times, slowly, and as she read, the colour began to come back to her pale face, like morning returning to a dark room. It was the first hope she had known for a year, and she held it close, afraid that it might vanish as quickly as it had come.

Rachel wrote back that very evening, in a few short and shaking lines, to say that she would come to Yorkshire and see the experiment with her own eyes. She would watch from a hiding-place, she wrote, so that Franklin should not be disturbed, and she hoped with all her heart that Ezra Jennings was right. Franklin read the answer ten times, and then he folded it very small and put it in the pocket nearest his heart.

The old sitting-room was put back exactly as it had been on the night of the birthday, with the cabinet in its corner, a false stone in the drawer and the smeared paint on the door. Betteredge supervised every chair and cushion, for he remembered the position of each as clearly as his own name. It was a strange feeling, as of walking back into a year-old dream, and it made even the old steward shiver.

To make every condition the same, Franklin gave up his cigars a second time, and for several days he slept as badly as he had done in the summer of the birthday. He was a miserable and irritable companion, but he accepted his misery without complaint, because the whole of his future depended on it. Betteredge watched him with great sympathy, and he offered a good many cups of tea that Franklin was too cross to drink.

On the evening of the experiment, Rachel arrived at dusk in a closed carriage, veiled and silent, and Mr Bruff met her at the door and led her quietly upstairs. He took her to a hiding-place where she could see everything without being seen, and she thanked him in a whisper. Her cheeks were burning, and her hands were cold as ice, and she gripped the arm of the lawyer who walked beside her.

At the usual hour Ezra measured out the dose with great care, exactly as the doctor had given it a year before, and he mixed it into a glass of brandy and water. Franklin looked at it for a moment, said, “Here is to the truth,” and drank it to the last drop before going up to his bed. Nobody in the room breathed freely, and the clock on the mantelpiece seemed to tick louder than it had ever done before.

Ezra and Mr Bruff took their places in the dark passage outside Franklin's door and waited, with only a shaded lamp between them. The hours passed very slowly, and the only sound in the great silent house was the ticking of the old clock in the hall below. Mr Bruff, who was not a patient man, found it harder than any trial he had ever conducted.

Late in the night the door opened slowly, and Franklin appeared on the threshold in his nightclothes, with his eyes wide open but fixed on nothing at all. He did not seem to see the two men who sat in the shadows, though they could have touched him, and he moved like a man walking at the bottom of a deep sea. Mr Bruff caught his breath, and for the first time in his long career he felt entirely at a loss for a clever remark.

Franklin walked slowly down the passage and along the dark landing, then down the stairs and across the hall, with the two watchers following him on tiptoe at a safe distance. He went by exactly the same way that he had gone a year before, without a single hesitation or mistake, and Ezra whispered that it was a sign. The moon was shining through the windows, exactly as it had shone on that other night, and it made long pale squares on the floor.

Franklin entered the sitting-room, walked directly to the cabinet, opened the little drawer and lifted out the false diamond which had been placed there for the experiment. In her hiding-place Rachel watched him with her hand pressed over her mouth, and silent tears ran down her face, for she was seeing again what she had seen a year before. It was exactly the same, and yet everything was different, for this time she knew that he was not to blame.

Franklin carried the false diamond back along the passage and up the stairs to his own room, exactly as he must have done a year before, and laid it carefully down. Then he lay upon his bed like a man who has finished a long and wearisome task, and he fell almost at once into a deep, untroubled sleep. The two watchers stood motionless in the doorway, hardly daring to breathe, while the sleeper settled himself among his pillows.

Mr Bruff took Ezra's thin hand in the grey light of the passage and admitted, with an honesty that did him credit, that he had been wrong to doubt. The experiment had proved beyond argument that Franklin could rise from his bed, act with perfect purpose and remember nothing whatever afterwards. Ezra only smiled his tired, gentle smile, and said that he had never doubted what the night would show.

Rachel stepped out of her hiding-place into the grey light of the dawn, and her face was wet with tears that she did not trouble to hide. She understood at last that Franklin had never meant to steal from her, that he had been as much a victim as she was, and that for a whole year she had wronged him. The knowledge came upon her like a great wave, and it swept away in a moment all the bitterness of the long year.

Franklin woke at sunrise with a heavy head and a dry mouth, and when he opened his eyes, he saw Rachel standing at the side of his bed with the early light on her hair. For a moment he thought that he was still dreaming, and he was afraid to speak in case the vision should vanish. She smiled at him through her tears, and it was the first time that he had seen her smile since the birthday.

Rachel begged him to forgive her for believing the worst of him, and Franklin, who had waited a year for that moment, took her into his arms without a word. There was nothing to forgive, he told her at last, for he had never for one hour stopped loving her, and the dawn seemed to come into the room just then. Mr Bruff turned his back and blew his nose, and he declared that the morning air in the country was most irritating.

Then they understood at last why Rosanna had hidden the stained nightgown in the sand, and why she had been so strange and secret in the days that followed. She had loved Franklin in silence, she had found the proof against him, and she had done everything in her power to save him. Rachel wept for her, and Franklin wept with her, and neither of them thought it any shame to do so.

When the first joy had settled a little, Franklin said quietly that the real diamond was still missing, and that nothing in the experiment could tell them where it had gone. If he had carried the stone to his own room that night in his sleep, someone must have come after him and taken it away. The question hung in the air, unanswered, and the pleasure of the dawn grew a little cooler as they considered it.

Mr Bruff observed thoughtfully that whoever had taken the stone from Franklin's room must have known where it was and must have seen him walk, and that it was time to call upon an expert. The man he had in mind was Sergeant Cuff, who had understood more about the case than anybody else, and who had, he said, been right about nearly everything. Nobody disagreed with him, for in that room there was only one man whom everyone trusted to find the truth.

Sergeant Cuff had retired from his profession and now lived in a pretty cottage in Dorking, where he spent his days among his roses and his evenings among the newspapers. Mr Bruff wrote to him at once, telling him all that had happened and begging him to come and listen. The reply came back by return of post, and it was brief and cordial.

Cuff arrived the next day with a fresh rose in his button-hole and a look of quiet interest on his thin, grey face, and he listened to the whole account of the experiment without once interrupting. When it was finished, he said that it was the most curious case that he had met in thirty years, and that he was delighted to be back. His eyes shone, and for the first time in a year or more he looked like a man who was truly happy.

Cuff began by asking, in his soft voice, who else had slept in the house on the night of the birthday, and who might have seen Franklin walking through the dark. The list, once Betteredge's old letters were fetched, was not long, and one name on it made the detective pause. He wrote it down in his black notebook and underlined it twice, but he said nothing to the others about what it meant.

Mr Bruff remembered the strange look that had crossed Godfrey's face when the terms of Lady Verinder's will were read, and he described it exactly to the detective. Cuff asked very quietly whether anybody knew if Mr Godfrey Ablewhite had troubles with his money, and nobody could say. The detective nodded and said that he would soon find out, for there were few secrets in London that money could not discover.
