Cuff set his helpers to ask careful questions in every corner of London, and within a week he returned with remarkable news. The charming Godfrey Ablewhite kept a second household in a villa at Northwood, which cost him a great deal of money, and he had kept it secret from every friend and relative he possessed. Miss Clack, had she known, would have fainted, and she would certainly have dropped a number of leaflets on the floor.

Cuff also learned that Godfrey, under all his charming speeches, had quietly spent a very large sum of money that he held in trust for another person, and that it must be paid back by a certain day. He had no means of finding it by honest work, and the day was drawing steadily nearer. Mr Bruff listened with his lips pressed together, and he did not interrupt once until the whole tale had been told.

Cuff laid out his theory for Franklin, Rachel and Mr Bruff with quiet, patient care, speaking as if he were setting out the pieces of a puzzle on a table. Godfrey, who had slept under the same roof that night, must have seen Franklin carrying the stone through the dark, and he had walked into the sleeper's room later and taken it for himself. It was a cruel and clever theory, and it explained every single fact that had puzzled them since the night of the birthday.

A stone like that was far too famous to be sold, Cuff pointed out, so Godfrey would have borrowed money by leaving it as a pledge with someone who asked no questions. The man for such work, in his experience, was Mr Luker, a moneylender in Lambeth, and he intended to watch Mr Luker's house without delay. His plan was simple and very patient, and it depended only on the weakness of a man who owed too much.

Cuff sent a sharp, quick-eyed boy named Gooseberry to watch Mr Luker's house from a doorway across the street, day and night, in every kind of weather. After a few days the lad returned with a report that surprised even the detective, for he had seen three tall men in dark clothes watching the same house. Cuff smiled grimly and did not speak, for he had been expecting just such a report for a long time.

Gooseberry also reported that Mr Luker had left his house in a great hurry, carrying a small packet under his arm, and had gone straight to his bank in Lombard Street. Cuff was certain at once that the diamond was now locked in the bank's strong-room, in the care of men who knew nothing about its history. The long search had narrowed to a single door, and Cuff felt, as he always did at such moments, a quiet and cold excitement.

On the day when the loan was due, Cuff and his helpers took their places near the bank in Lombard Street, and they watched every man who went in or came out with the patience of cats outside a mouse-hole. Mr Bruff stood in a doorway with a newspaper held in front of his face, and Gooseberry sat on a step with a bag of nuts. The street was loud with traffic and the clatter of wheels, but the watchers saw and heard nothing except the bank door.

At noon, Godfrey Ablewhite arrived in a cab, looking pale, anxious and much older than he had looked in Yorkshire, and he went into the bank without glancing about. A few minutes later he came out again, having found the money and repaid Mr Luker, with a small packet buttoned inside his coat. Cuff, in his doorway, did not stir a muscle, and he waited until the cab had moved away before he gave his signal.

Godfrey came out of the bank in a great hurry, glancing nervously behind him at every corner, as though he feared something far worse than the police. Gooseberry slipped after him through the crowds like a shadow, never losing sight of the hurrying figure, while Cuff followed at a distance with an air of the greatest calm. The chase led across half of London, through narrow lanes and crowded markets, and ended at last in a shabby quiet street.

At last Godfrey reached Tolliver's, a quiet old inn on the edge of the city, where he signed the visitors' book under a false name and asked for a room at the back. He meant to leave England as soon as he could find a ship, and he hoped that no one in the world knew where he had gone. He was wrong on both counts, as he would find before the night was over, for he had been followed from the very beginning.

Late that night, the three Indians who had followed Godfrey patiently across London slipped silently into the inn and into his room, as softly as three shadows. They had waited for a year, for years upon years, for fifty years and more, and they were in no hurry now that the stone was within their reach. The old inn made no sound, and the only witness to the visit was the pale light of the lamp in the passage.

In the morning the servants of the inn found Godfrey Ablewhite dead in his bed, quite peacefully, and the small packet that he had carried so anxiously was gone from his coat. The Indians had taken what they came for, they had left no trace behind them, and no one in the whole of the old inn had heard so much as a footstep. The news was sent at once to Cuff, who came to the inn in a cab with an expression that showed nothing at all.

Cuff and Mr Bruff were called to the inn without delay, and they stood side by side at the bedside in grave silence, looking at the quiet face. Though the name in the visitors' book was false, they knew the dead man at once as Godfrey Ablewhite, the gentle speaker, the friend of so many good causes, whose secret life had ended in a shabby room. Mr Bruff took off his hat, for even a lawyer may pay respect to a man who has paid so dearly for his mistakes.

The three Indians sailed from England by the next outward-bound ship, and Cuff explained to the others, in his sad, unhurried way, that they had done only what their oath required of them. They had followed their god's stone across the world for half a century, and now they were carrying it home to put right the old wrong. Mr Bruff admitted that there was a dreadful justice in it, though he added that he would rather not have seen the end.

In the spring, Franklin and Rachel were married in the village church near the old house, with Mr Bruff, Penelope and old Betteredge in the front row. The steward wept openly, blew his nose like a trumpet and declared that it was only the draught from the door, and no one believed him for a moment. It was the happiest day that the house had seen for years, and the bells rang out over the fields until the sun went down.

Some time later, a letter arrived from Mr Murthwaite, who had returned to India, and who had been present at a great festival in the western province of Kattiawar. Among the crowds of pilgrims he had recognised three men with shaven heads and plain robes, and he had known them instantly by their calm and upright bearing. They were the three guardians of the moon god, who had followed the stone through half a century of travel and trouble.

Mr Murthwaite wrote that he had watched the three men carry the stone in solemn procession to the holy city of Somnauth, with a great crowd of pilgrims bowing low as they passed. No one dared to touch it, and no one dared to speak, and when the stone entered the temple, the whole hillside fell as silent as the moon. It was a sight that he would never forget, and he wrote that he was glad to have lived to see it.

Once more the great yellow diamond shone in the forehead of the moon god, in the place where it had shone for centuries before the soldiers came, and the three priests knelt in the lamplight before it. Nobody in England would ever see it again, and perhaps that was best, for the stone had brought nothing to those who took it but sorrow and fear. The Moonstone had come home at last, and the long and troubled journey of a stone that nobody could own came quietly to an end.
